strategy_title: Develop a rigorous framework for measuring AI agent reliability
strategy_text: Investigate how autonomous and semi-autonomous AI agents can be measured objectively, reproducibly, and meaningfully across diverse tasks and operating conditions. Build an evaluation framework that distinguishes superficial task completion from correctness, robustness, and dependable behavior. Audit representative agent benchmarks for task-selection effects, environmental variability, evaluator bias, contamination, and weak completion oracles. Define operational measures for end-to-end success, partial completion, error severity, recovery, repeat-trial consistency, tool-use correctness, and resources per successful outcome. Specify how to evaluate stochastic agents, long dependency chains, long-running tasks, external tools, and changing environments. Propose repeated-trial protocols, uncertainty intervals, failure-distribution reporting, and comparisons under controlled compute, time, tool, and monetary budgets. State the evidence and replication needed for defensible reliability claims; separate benchmark-specific gains from general improvements. Deliver a protocol with task strata, outcome rubrics, baseline comparisons, statistical analysis, and explicit limits on what its results can establish.

strategy_runs.strategy_title: Understand failure propagation and recovery in autonomous AI agents
strategy_runs.strategy_text: Map how agents fail during extended, multi-step tasks and determine which failures are detectable, recoverable, or silently corrupt later results. Examine incorrect reasoning and plans, tool misuse, incomplete observations, stale or compressed context, instruction misunderstandings, environmental changes, and accumulated state errors. Trace concrete failure chains from initiating fault through subsequent actions to user-visible consequences; distinguish model limitations from architecture, orchestration, memory, interface, and environment failures. Investigate detection of silent errors, calibrated uncertainty versus actual failure, retry and replanning policies, escalation, and safe termination. Analyze checkpointing, state reconstruction, independent verification, rollback, idempotency, and human intervention as recovery mechanisms. For each mechanism, specify assumptions, failure modes, and measurable recovery criteria; compare recovery against restarting and continuing without intervention. Develop fault-injection scenarios and trace-based analyses that reveal propagation and test whether recovery restores correct state rather than merely producing a plausible answer. Deliver a failure taxonomy, causal workflow maps, and a prioritized set of falsifiable experiments, distinguishing observed evidence from proposed mechanisms.

strategy_runs.strategy_title: Test architectural mechanisms for dependable agent outcomes
strategy_runs.strategy_text: Compare architectural interventions intended to improve agent reliability, including constrained tool interfaces, typed action and observation schemas, explicit state and provenance, planning and execution separation, checkpoints, bounded retries, independent verification, uncertainty-triggered escalation, sandboxing, and safe stopping. Select representative multi-step tasks and controlled perturbations involving tool errors, partial observations, stale data, environment changes, and ambiguous instructions. Establish a transparent baseline and change one mechanism at a time before testing justified combinations. Measure verified task success, severity-weighted errors, silent failures, recovery rate, consistency, latency, token/tool use, and cost per verified success. Use repeated trials and report uncertainty; control model version, prompts, tools, budgets, task difficulty, and environment wherever feasible. Test whether gains persist on held-out tasks and under distribution shifts, and whether interventions introduce new failure modes or merely shift costs. Separate implemented and empirically evaluated mechanisms from conceptual proposals; do not infer causal benefit from correlations or a single benchmark. Deliver an evidence table linking each mechanism to its assumptions, measured effects, costs, regressions, and unresolved validation needs.

strategy_snapshot.title: Develop a rigorous framework for measuring AI agent reliability
Understand failure propagation and recovery in autonomous AI agents
Test architectural mechanisms for dependable agent outcomes

problem:
Autonomous AI agents are increasingly expected to complete complex tasks involving planning, reasoning, external tools, persistent state, and interaction with changing environments. Demonstrations and benchmark results show that agents can perform many such tasks, but provide limited evidence that they remain dependable across repeated executions, unfamiliar conditions, long-running workflows, and settings where mistakes have significant consequences. This project asks how autonomous and semi-autonomous agents can be evaluated and engineered to deliver reliable, correct, recoverable, and reproducible results across extended, multi-step tasks.

Agent reliability is a system-level property. Probabilistic decisions, dynamically constructed plans, incomplete observations, tool interfaces, memory, orchestration, and external state all affect whether the intended outcome is actually achieved. Small errors can propagate through later actions and yield plausible but incorrect results. An agent may claim completion without satisfying the task, recover from one failure while introducing another, or behave differently across otherwise comparable runs. Reliability therefore cannot be inferred from fluent explanations, a single successful trajectory, agreement among similar models, or benchmark scores alone.

Investigate three connected questions. First, how should reliability be defined and measured so evaluation reflects actual correctness, robustness, consistency, recoverability, tool-use quality, and cost rather than superficial completion? Second, what are the principal sources of failure, how do errors propagate through multi-step execution, and which signals and interventions can detect, contain, or recover from failures without creating additional risks? Third, which engineering mechanisms demonstrably improve outcomes, and how can their effects be established through controlled experiments rather than architectural intuition or anecdotal success? The strategies approach these questions from complementary measurement, failure-analysis, and intervention perspectives; none presumes a preferred architecture.

Use available research literature, software-reliability principles, empirical evaluation methods, and documented agent-system designs. Examine the relationship between model capability and end-to-end system reliability, including tool interfaces, state management, verification, orchestration, uncertainty handling, changing environments, recovery, and execution budgets. Assess benchmark sensitivity to task selection, evaluator bias, contamination, and weak completion oracles. Consider stochastic behavior, repeated trials, long dependency chains, held-out tasks, fault injection, independent correctness judgments, and uncertainty in estimated success rates. Where comparisons are proposed, make assumptions and controls explicit, including model and prompt versions, task difficulty, environment, tool access, compute, latency, and monetary budgets.

Evaluate competing approaches on the strength and limits of their evidence. Distinguish measured results from formal or theoretical arguments, proposed mechanisms, and unsupported claims; do not present planned experiments as completed or infer causal benefit from correlation. Account for correlated errors among agents or critics that share models and training data, and for the difficulty of constructing an independent oracle for open-ended tasks. Analyze tradeoffs among reliability, flexibility, recovery overhead, latency, and computational expense, including cases where a safeguard shifts rather than removes risk.

The intended outcome is an evidence-grounded account of what reliability claims current evaluations can support, a practical and reproducible evaluation framework, a causal taxonomy of important failure and recovery modes, and architectural principles whose limits are explicit. Identify unresolved questions and specify discriminating experiments needed to validate competing claims. The project is open-ended: conclusions should remain proportional to the quality, independence, and generality of available evidence.

output.claim: Conditional finite-panel audit lemma: after a fixed roster of M paired agent executions has finished, a uniformly random audit of m pairs can give a valid one-sided confidence bound on the roster's actual success-rate difference without assuming independence among execution outcomes. Conservative treatment of unresolved audit labels preserves coverage. This certifies only the frozen roster—not deployment reliability—and requires sound outcome evidence rather than agreement among judges.
output.method: Derive an exact randomization-based audit certificate using hypergeometric inversion. Hypothesis: randomized post-execution auditing can separate uncertainty about a realized evaluation panel from assumptions about independent task sampling. The discriminating outcome is coverage over audit selection for every fixed binary outcome roster, including perfectly correlated executions and adversarially unresolved labels. A subsequent test should enumerate all audits of small rosters and then apply the protocol to an instrumented external-state task. No runtime or external sources are available, so neither test was executed. The ledger's sampling, missing-label, and reference-validity obligations motivate this result; their original source artifacts are pointer-only and were not inspected. The supplied recovery extract is reviewed only within its stated scope; its invalid delivery relaxation is rejected, not transferred into this measurement result. Prior provider errors, timeout, and cancellation motivate a bounded standalone derivation rather than repeating an unavailable execution request.

reasoning_steps.title: Separate the current measurement question from incomplete historical evidence
reasoning_steps.argument: The supplied extract of fdfb1b57-9f8a-451c-b9b4-2cca9cbf618f concerns ambiguous external writes, not statistical audit coverage. Its correction is concrete: if all retries are dropped, issuing a retry need not duplicate an already committed operation; therefore the inequality Pr(success|W1) <= 1-q cannot be retained without the retry-commitment premise or a newly justified replacement. I reject that relaxation and leave its crash-boundary extension unresolved. I adopt only the measurement lesson that an agent's local completion report does not determine actual external-state correctness. The statistical artifacts referenced by the ledger are not supplied originals, so no historical bound is assumed here.

reasoning_steps.title: Define a finite, realized target rather than an unobserved deployment population
reasoning_steps.argument: Freeze M >= 1 scheduled pairs after execution and before drawing the audit. For pair i, let Y_Ai and Y_Bi be binary satisfaction of a prespecified actual-outcome rubric at a fixed horizon, including required external effects and reporting correctness. Define G_i = 1{Y_Ai=1,Y_Bi=0}, L_i = 1{Y_Ai=0,Y_Bi=1}, G = sum_i G_i, and L = sum_i L_i. The target is Delta_panel = M^(-1) sum_i(Y_Ai-Y_Bi) = (G-L)/M. All execution outcomes may be dependent. This is a descriptive paired contrast; without controlled assignment it is not a causal effect. Unexecuted scheduled slots must have a prespecified operational score, such as incomplete, rather than being silently removed or treated as observed hypothetical executions.

reasoning_steps.title: Use audit randomness, not execution independence
reasoning_steps.argument: Independently of the frozen outcomes, draw an m-element subset uniformly without replacement from the M pairs, where 1 <= m <= M. If the audited gains and losses were fully known, their counts X_G and X_L would each have a hypergeometric marginal distribution: Pr_K(X=x) = binom(K,x) binom(M-K,m-x) / binom(M,m), with K respectively G or L and out-of-range binomial coefficients zero. This follows by counting subsets containing x of the K marked pairs. It requires no independence between X_G and X_L, nor between any agent executions.

reasoning_steps.title: Construct exact directional count bounds
reasoning_steps.argument: Fix 0 < alpha < 1 and a = alpha/2. Write T_K(x) = Pr_K(X >= x) and F_K(x) = Pr_K(X <= x). Define ell(x) = min{K in {0,...,M}: T_K(x) > a} and u(x) = max{K in {0,...,M}: F_K(x) > a}. These sets are nonempty: K=M makes the upper-tail probability one, and K=0 makes the lower-tail probability one for any 0 <= x <= m. Coupling populations by adding marked items shows X is stochastically increasing in K; therefore T_K increases and F_K decreases with K. Both ell and u are nondecreasing functions of the observed count.

reasoning_steps.title: Prove marginal coverage and combine it without assuming independent labels
reasoning_steps.argument: For true K, ell(X)>K implies T_K(X)<=a. Because T_K(x) decreases in x, the event T_K(X)<=a is an upper-tail event whose probability is at most a: if its smallest attainable count is c, its probability is T_K(c)<=a; if no such count exists it is zero. Likewise, u(X)<K implies F_K(X)<=a, a lower-tail event of probability at most a. Consequently Pr(ell(X_G)<=G) >= 1-a and Pr(L<=u(X_L)) >= 1-a. The union bound gives simultaneous validity at least 1-alpha, regardless of dependence between these events. On this event, Delta_panel >= [ell(X_G)-u(X_L)]/M.

reasoning_steps.title: Handle missing or disputed audit labels by sound sets of possible outcomes
reasoning_steps.argument: For each audited pair, record a nonempty set C_i contained in {00,01,10,11} that contains its actual outcome, with coordinates ordered A,B. A certified gain requires C_i={10}; a possible loss means 01 belongs to C_i. Let g_cert count certified gains and l_pos count possible losses. Pointwise, g_cert<=X_G and l_pos>=X_L. Monotonicity then gives ell(g_cert)<=ell(X_G) and u(l_pos)>=u(X_L). Thus the reported lower bound B = [ell(g_cert)-u(l_pos)]/M is no larger than the fully labeled bound and retains coverage at least 1-alpha. This remains true even if which labels become unresolved depends on outcomes or on the chosen audit subset. Completely missing evidence receives C_i={00,01,10,11}; missing labels are not dropped. The essential premise is containment of the actual outcome, not the confidence or agreement of adjudicators.

reasoning_steps.title: Check census and no-information edge cases
reasoning_steps.argument: If m=M, the hypergeometric sample count equals K deterministically, giving ell(x)=u(x)=x. With fully resolved labels, B equals Delta_panel exactly. With unresolved labels, the census bound becomes (g_cert-l_pos)/M, the minimum compatible contrast: choose outcome 01 wherever it remains possible, choose a nongain elsewhere unless 10 is forced. If every audited pair is completely unresolved, g_cert=0 and l_pos=m, so ell(0)=0, u(m)=M, and B=-1. The procedure therefore does not manufacture positive evidence from missing or ungrounded labels.

reasoning_steps.title: Identify what this certificate cannot establish
reasoning_steps.argument: A positive B supports only that A's realized panel success rate exceeds B's at confidence at least 1-alpha over the randomized audit. It does not show that the panel represents deployment tasks, that future executions have the same distribution, that A caused an improvement, or that a binary rubric captures delayed harm. Audit randomization also cannot repair unsound outcome sets: without any connection to actual outcomes, the same observed reports can accompany all pairs being 10 or all pairs being 01, yielding contrasts +1 and -1. Independent state inspection or another justified outcome constraint is therefore necessary for a nontrivial actual-correctness claim. Execution-cluster independence is avoided for this finite-panel target, not established for any population target.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify the bounded discriminating test and practical reporting protocol
reasoning_steps.argument: When execution becomes available, enumerate all outcome rosters for M<=6 and all audit subsets for each m, compute B from exact hypergeometric probabilities, and verify that the fraction of subsets with B>Delta_panel is at most alpha. Include perfectly correlated outcomes, all-gain/all-loss controls, a census, and outcome-dependent label masking; verify masking never increases B. For an applied pilot, freeze versions, prompts, budgets, pair roster, rubric, horizon, audit size, and random seed before inspection; draw the audit only after the panel is frozen. Use an instrumented append service with an independently retained operation ledger to distinguish absent, single, and duplicate effects, retaining ambiguous cases as outcome sets. Report B, unresolved-label counts, omissions, severity categories, and total execution-plus-audit costs. This is a proposed test, not measured coverage or an engineering-benefit result.

assumptions: A finite roster of M paired execution slots, their actual binary rubric outcomes, and the observation horizon are fixed before audit selection; audit inspection does not change those outcomes.
Every scheduled slot remains in the denominator, with prespecified operational treatment of nonexecution; the claim does not concern hypothetical outcomes of omitted executions.
The m audited pairs form a uniformly random subset without replacement, independent of the frozen outcomes, with 1 <= m <= M.
Every audited possible-outcome set contains the actual pair outcome. A disputed or unavailable label is represented conservatively rather than assumed correct.
The confidence level satisfies 0 < alpha < 1 and is fixed before inspecting audit outcomes.
output.evidence_status: Standalone conditional mathematical derivation using standard finite-population sampling techniques; no computation, benchmark audit, literature inspection, independent verification, or empirical calibration was performed. This advances finite-panel measurement and conservative missing-label handling, not population generalization or causal engineering evaluation. output.claim: Conditional recovery result: for one logical operation, a durable stable key plus a serializable, atomic effect-and-completion-record transaction prevents duplicate effects; eventual request processing and response delivery additionally give eventual verified completion, but not completion by a fixed deadline H. Stable keys alone do not suffice when effect and completion-record writes are non-atomic. Regenerating keys after ambiguous outcomes defeats even the atomic implementation. The six-case crash analysis below establishes these statements within an explicit service model, not for deployed tools.
output.method: Correct the supplied prior argument's delivery-relaxation error, then derive crash-prefix transitions for three service implementations crossed with stable versus regenerated keys. Hypothesis: both key continuity and atomic coupling of the actual effect to its completion record are needed for the stated recovery guarantee. The discriminator is independently audited external-effect count and receipt validity after recovery, not the agent's completion claim. Hold payload, logical operation, initial state, retry schedule, and crash position fixed across implementations; use no-crash and no-retry controls. The transition analysis is analytical, not an executed experiment. Both runtimes are unavailable, so no computation is requested. Recorded timeout/cancellation failures motivate a bounded standalone analysis, not repetition of an unavailable execution. Operational failures are not mathematical evidence.

reasoning_steps.title: Scope of historical evidence and correction
reasoning_steps.argument: The supplied extract of fdfb1b57-9f8a-451c-b9b4-2cca9cbf618f exposes a specific invalid sentence: dropping assured retry commitment does not preserve Pr(success in W1) <= 1-q, where q is retry probability. An always-retry policy whose retries all disappear has q=1, yet the already-committed history W1 retains exactly one effect. Retract that relaxation. The original conditional bound retains its original delivery premise: success in W0 requires retry, while success in W1 excludes retry when every retry commits. Nothing here establishes that the same bound holds under arbitrary relaxed delivery. The original artifact is unavailable; this correction addresses only the explicitly supplied argument and objection.

reasoning_steps.title: Define observable success and service state
reasoning_steps.argument: Consider one initially unperformed logical operation with a fixed payload. Let C count its irreversible durable effects across all keys, and let e_k count effects under key k. Let d_k be a durable terminal completion record containing the payload and a success receipt. Initially C=e_k=d_k=0. External-state correctness at H means C(H)=1; full task completion additionally requires an accurate terminal report by H. C=0, C>=2, and escalation are separate outcomes. Each actual effect increments C and its e_k by one. A service receipt is not assumed accurate merely because it exists.

reasoning_steps.title: Define implementation and crash semantics
reasoning_steps.argument: On a request, the service checks d_k. If present with matching payload, it returns the cached receipt without executing an effect; mismatched payloads are rejected. For an absent record, A atomically commits effect E and record D; ED persists E before D; DE persists D before E. D is treated as completed, not as a pending intent. Crashes retain durable writes but discard the interrupted handler, and there is no background repair of partial ED or DE operations. Requests are serialized, so concurrency is not needed for the counterexamples. Replies normally follow the whole sequence. For the crash table, retry processing has no further crash and completes if it is not suppressed by D.

reasoning_steps.title: Define the two key policies and table interpretation
reasoning_steps.argument: Stable means the operation-to-key-and-payload mapping is durable before the first send and every retry reuses that key. Regenerated means recovery sends the same logical operation under a fresh unused key. Each table case starts from an unused key, runs the original request to a specified durable boundary, loses the reply or crashes, and then retries once. Reported counts are after that retry is handled. For A the possible boundaries are before and after its atomic commit; a crash during the transaction has one of those durable outcomes. For ED they are before E, between E and D, and after D. For DE they are before D, between D and E, and after E. A crash after reply delivery but before durable local completion produces the same retry cases if the local pending record survives.

reasoning_steps.title: Crash table: atomic service with a stable key
reasoning_steps.argument: A × stable: before commit, (e_k,d_k)=(0,0), so retry commits (1,1), yielding C=1. After commit, (1,1), so retry returns the cached receipt and leaves C=1. No durable (1,0) or (0,1) state exists. Thus every crash boundary yields one effect after a completed retry. At the client boundary, retaining and reusing the same pending key preserves this argument even when the first reply was received but local completion was not recorded.

reasoning_steps.title: Crash table: atomic service with a regenerated key
reasoning_steps.argument: A × regenerated: a pre-commit crash leaves C=0, and a fresh-key retry gives C=1. A post-commit crash leaves C=1 and d_k=1, but the fresh key k' has d_k'=0; its atomic transaction increments C to 2. Concrete chain: original atomic commit → lost acknowledgment → restored pending task → new key → second atomic commit. Atomicity protects each key, not the logical operation across different keys.

reasoning_steps.title: Crash table: effect-before-record with a stable key
reasoning_steps.argument: ED × stable: before E, retry yields C=1. Between E and D, durable state is (e_k,d_k)=(1,0); retry sees no record, executes another E, and then writes D, yielding C=2. After D, retry is suppressed and C stays 1. Consequently the boundary outcomes are 1, 2, 1. The middle trace refutes the candidate claim that stable keys and a deduplication table alone guarantee at-most-once effects.

reasoning_steps.title: Crash table: effect-before-record with a regenerated key
reasoning_steps.argument: ED × regenerated: before E, the fresh-key retry yields C=1. Between E and D, the original effect already exists and the fresh-key retry adds another, yielding C=2. After D, the original complete operation likewise does not suppress a fresh-key request, yielding C=2. The boundary outcomes are 1, 2, 2. Fixing key continuity removes the last failure but not the non-atomic middle-window failure.

reasoning_steps.title: Crash table: record-before-effect with a stable key
reasoning_steps.argument: DE × stable: before D, retry executes the full sequence and yields C=1. Between D and E, durable state is (e_k,d_k)=(0,1); retry returns the cached success receipt without E, leaving C=0. With no repair process, all subsequent same-key retries remain suppressed. After E, retry is suppressed and C stays 1. The boundary outcomes are 1, 0, 1. This middle trace produces a successful-looking receipt with no actual effect, demonstrating why receipt counts cannot serve as the sole correctness oracle.

reasoning_steps.title: Crash table: record-before-effect with a regenerated key
reasoning_steps.argument: DE × regenerated: before D, the fresh-key retry yields C=1. Between D and E, the abandoned original has no effect; the fresh-key retry yields C=1 but leaves an invalid old completion record. After E, the original effect exists and the fresh-key retry yields C=2. The boundary outcomes are 1, 1, 2. The middle outcome is externally correct only under the stipulated absence of repair or resumption of the old handler; it does not establish a generally safe recovery policy.

reasoning_steps.title: General invariant and eventual-completion direction

If the policy always retries but every retry is dropped, then q=1 while the second history still has exactly one effect: its external-state correctness probability is 1, not at most 0. reasoning_steps.title: Define the service and recovery contracts
reasoning_steps.argument: Analyze one logical operation with fixed payload x, initially no effects or receipts. Let C count its irreversible durable external effects and R[k] denote a durable terminal success receipt for key k. Each individual effect and receipt write is atomic. Service attempts are serialized, and restart abandons volatile unfinished work. There is no background reconciliation, compensation, expiry, or other deduplication. An existing R[k] returns cached success without creating an effect; reuse with a different payload is rejected. Atomic implementation A commits one effect and R[k] in one indivisible durable transition. Implementation E commits the effect and then R[k]. Implementation R commits R[k] and then the effect. Responses are sent after the intended sequence, except that replay can return an existing receipt. A stable-key client durably records (k,x) before its first send and reuses it; a regenerating client uses a fresh key after ambiguous recovery. These definitions intentionally exclude stronger split-write implementations with durable repair protocols.

reasoning_steps.title: Crash-boundary transition table
reasoning_steps.argument:
Write state as (C, receipt present for the original key). B0 is before any durable transition; B1 is between split writes; B2 is after all writes but before an acknowledgment reaches the client. A has no B1. The following table describes a subsequent retry that runs to completion; K means reuse the original key and N means use a fresh key.
Implementation/key | B0 retry | B1 crash then retry | B2 acknowledgment loss then retry
A/K | (0,0) -> (1,1) | impossible boundary | (1,1) -> (1,1), cached response
A/N | (0,0) -> one effect under new key | impossible boundary | original effect plus new-key effect: C=2
E/K | (0,0) -> (1,1) | (1,0) -> (2,1): duplicate | (1,1) -> (1,1), cached response
E/N | (0,0) -> one effect under new key | original effect plus new-key effect: C=2 | original effect plus new-key effect: C=2
R/K | (0,0) -> (1,1) | (0,1) -> (0,1): cached success, omitted effect | (1,1) -> (1,1), cached response
R/N | (0,0) -> one effect under new key | old receipt remains; new-key attempt produces C=1 | original effect plus new-key effect: C=2
For N rows, the new receipt belongs to the new key; C always aggregates the same logical operation. After a received acknowledgment and durable local completion, no retry is required. A client crash before saving that completion reduces to B2.

reasoning_steps.title: Prove the atomic stable-key safety invariant
reasoning_steps.argument: For A/K define Ck as the number of effects committed with the sole operation key. Initially Ck=0 and R[k] is absent. An interrupted atomic transition leaves either that state or the committed state Ck=1 with R[k] present. From the committed state every replay only returns the receipt. No transition removes the receipt or increments Ck again. Induction over any finite sequence of attempts and crashes therefore gives Ck in {0,1} and R[k] present if and only if Ck=1. The same safety statement holds throughout an infinite execution because every violation would have a finite first occurrence. As every send for this logical operation uses k, C=Ck and duplication is impossible. Serialization is an explicit premise; a concurrent implementation must supply equivalent linearizable atomic behavior.

reasoning_steps.argument: E/K loses the information needed to recognize an already committed effect: crash after the effect but before its receipt, followed by a complete same-key retry, creates two effects. A/N preserves the per-key invariant but not a per-logical-operation invariant: commit under k, lose acknowledgment, then commit under fresh k' gives one effect per key and two effects overall. E/N and R/N also admit this last complete-commit/lost-acknowledgment trace. Thus key regeneration may repair the particular R intermediate-crash omission, but it is not a generally safe recovery rule. These traces do not refute split-write designs with additional recovery mechanisms excluded by the model, nor establish that atomicity is necessary in every possible design.

reasoning_steps.title: Define finite retention, execution and concurrency
reasoning_steps.argument: One initially unperformed logical operation has a fixed payload p and a durably assigned key k. Every execution path for it uses k; keys are not reused. C counts all actual irreversible effects for the operation. A successful first execution at service time c atomically increments C and creates completion record D(k,p). Under the expiry-only implementation, D suppresses effects during [c,c+T), where T>0, and may be deleted at c+T; deletion does not undo the effect. An absent record again permits execution. Request handling, record deletion and effect commits have a per-key linearizable order consistent with service time. The suppressing-state check and actual effect are in the same atomic transition: a handler cannot retain an earlier absent observation as authority to execute later. Crashes expose either the entire durable transition or none of it. Service time is monotonic and the retention guarantee survives crashes. These are stipulated implementation properties, stronger than merely having a deduplication table.

reasoning_steps.title: Concrete expiry-induced duplicate after retry issuance stops
reasoning_steps.argument: Take T=10. At time 0 the client durably stores (operation,k,p) and sends request r1. At time 1, r1 commits one effect and D, so C=1; its acknowledgment is lost. At time 2 the client sends same-key retry r2. At time 3 it stops issuing retries, but r2 remains in flight. At time 11, D expires and is deleted. At time 12, r2 reaches its atomic execution transition, finds no D and commits another effect plus a new D, giving C=2. Both commits are atomic, the payload and key never change, and no concurrency or additional crash is needed. The chain is lost acknowledgment → retry already issued → client stops → suppression evidence expires → delayed execution → duplicate effect. This refutes the expiry-only candidate, not the earlier theorem with permanent retention.

reasoning_steps.title: Separate issuance, arrival and effective execution horizons
reasoning_steps.argument: Let S bound final request issuance, A bound final service ingress, and L bound every possible effect-capable atomic execution transition for this operation. An issuance bound S supplies neither A nor L without additional guarantees. Even A alone is insufficient: in the preceding trace, let r2 enter a service queue at time 2.5 but execute at time 12. Then every request has arrived before D expires, yet duplication still occurs. For a concrete sufficient timing construction, suppose all producers cease issuance by S, every transmitted copy arrives or is permanently discarded within Δ, and every arrived request commits its effect-capable transition or becomes irrevocably unable to execute within P of ingress. These bounds must include transport retries, queues, transaction retries, crashes and resumed work. Then A=S+Δ and L=S+Δ+P are valid upper bounds. A client timeout or an unacknowledged cancellation request establishes none of these server-side properties.

reasoning_steps.title: State sufficient contract A: retention dominates execution horizon
reasoning_steps.argument: In addition to the common atomic/stable-key premises, suppose no effect-capable transition for this operation can occur after a finite L. Every first committed effect at c must leave D available through all such later transitions; with deletion allowed at c+T, the strict condition c+T>L suffices. A configuration rule not requiring knowledge of c is: choose a known lower bound b on the first possible effect time and require b+T>L. Since c>=b, this implies c+T>L. For example, b can be the operation's earliest permitted send time, provided no earlier request can exist. Combining this with the previous timing construction gives the conservative rule T>S+Δ+P-b. These are sufficient conditions, not necessary conditions for every possible request schedule.

reasoning_steps.title: Prove contract A, including boundary cases
reasoning_steps.argument: If there is no committed effect, C=0 and safety holds. Otherwise let c be the first effect commit. Suppose a second effect commits at d in the per-key order. The execution-horizon premise gives d<=L, and retention gives L<c+T. The first commit installed D atomically; D cannot be deleted before c+T. Thus D is present at the second transition, which must suppress the effect, a contradiction. Overlapping requests cannot evade this argument because their atomic transitions are ordered and recheck suppressing state. After expiry there is no remaining effect-capable transition by the horizon premise. Crashes preserve the durable record and cannot create a partial commit. Equality needs explicit treatment: if c+T=L and deletion precedes a request at that same timestamp, a duplicate is possible. Strict inequality avoids relying on an unspecified tie order. Concurrent transitions at the same timestamp remain ordered by linearizability.

reasoning_steps.title: State sufficient contract B: retain suppression, expire only the result
reasoning_steps.argument: Alternatively, keep a durable tombstone B(k,p) indefinitely. The first successful execution atomically commits the actual effect, B and the full completion record D. Every effect-capable transition checks B within the same atomic transition: if B exists, it performs no effect; mismatching payloads are rejected. D may expire after T, but B is never removed, forgotten during failover, or bypassed by a worker. After D expires, a matching request may receive an explicit 'already applied; original result unavailable' response rather than a fabricated success receipt. All execution paths, including overlapping or resumed handlers, obey this gate. This branch does not require any bound on request delay.

reasoning_steps.title: Prove contract B by invariant
reasoning_steps.argument: Initially C=0 and B is absent. Induct over the linearized durable transitions. A rejected or suppressed request changes neither C nor B. A first successful request with B absent atomically changes (C,B) from (0,absent) to (1,present). No request with B present can increment C. Expiring D leaves B unchanged, and crashes preserve the durable state or leave an interrupted transaction uncommitted. Hence every finite execution prefix satisfies C∈{0,1} and B is present exactly when C=1. Arbitrarily late requests therefore cannot create a second effect. Installing B only after the effect would reopen the effect-before-record crash window; allowing any gap between deleting D and installing B would likewise invalidate this proof. Atomic installation at the original effect commit avoids both gaps.

reasoning_steps.title: Distinguish safe cessation, cancellation and verified completion
reasoning_steps.argument: Stopping retry issuance constrains future client sends, not requests already transmitted, queued or executing. To assert that no effect can occur after a cancellation acknowledgment, the service needs an additional contract: cancellation must fence every execution path at its atomic effect transition, and any already-committed effect must be reported rather than treated as cancelled. Merely stopping an agent or restoring a checkpoint does not provide that contract. Both proved branches establish only at-most-once safety. They permit C=0 forever, and neither guarantees truthful client completion by a deadline. In contract B, loss of D can remove result retrievability without removing duplicate suppression. Regenerating a key to recover a missing result remains unsafe. Consequently duplicate rate, omission rate, result availability and post-stop effects must be separate evaluation outcomes.

Add overlapping requests, crashes at first commit and D expiry, and failover with tombstone persistence. Independently count external effects and log issuance, ingress, atomic transition, expiry, cancellation acknowledgment and result availability. Hypothesis: finite retention is safe only when expired deduplication evidence cannot be followed by another effect-capable execution for the same logical operation. Discriminate the candidates using a concrete delayed-retry trace, a conditional safety proof, and a proposed expiry-boundary test comparing ordinary receipt expiry with a service-enforced execution deadline. Assume serialized atomic processing of the actual external effect and receipt, durable stable operation identity, and the clock contracts stated below. Scientific Python and SageMath remain unavailable; no implementation, execution, or empirical result is claimed. reasoning_steps.title: Define finite retention and its clock
reasoning_steps.argument: Consider one logical operation, fixed payload x, and one durably preserved key k; C counts all its irreversible external effects. Initially C=0 and no receipt exists. Use one authoritative service clock t, with a consistent ordering of processing and expiration events. It advances through outages, never rolls back across restart, and is coherent across any participating replicas. A first atomic commitment at time c creates the actual durable effect and receipt R[k]=(x, success, c, e), where e=c+T and T>0. The receipt is usable exactly while t<e; at t=e it is expired, even if physical garbage collection is delayed. Replays do not refresh e. Expiration never removes an effect. At a serialized processing transition, the service returns a valid matching receipt without an effect; absent such a receipt, the ordinary finite-retention implementation creates one effect and a new receipt atomically. Payload mismatches against a valid receipt are rejected. There is no other deduplication or repair.

reasoning_steps.title: Define delayed requests and crash recovery
reasoning_steps.argument: A send can be dropped, duplicated, or delayed in transport or service queues. Gateway arrival is not the effect-capable processing time. Any delayed copy may survive a client or service restart. Client recovery restores the same operation key and payload; where used, it also restores the original cutoff and deadline rather than resetting them. Service restart preserves committed effects, unexpired receipts, their original expiration times, and any execution-deadline enforcement. It abandons uncommitted atomic work; durable queues may later redeliver requests. Deduplication checks, execution-eligibility checks, and an effect-producing commit are one serialized transition, with no authorization cached across expiration or deadline passage. Without an additional bound, the last possible processing time of a request is unbounded.

reasoning_steps.title: Construct a stable-key duplication trace
reasoning_steps.argument: Take T=10 clock units. At t=1 the initial request atomically creates one effect and its receipt, so C=1 and e=11. Its acknowledgment is lost, and the client crashes before saving completion. Recovery restores the same (k,x), sends a retry at t=2, and sends nothing after a cutoff S=3. The retry remains queued. A service restart at t=10 preserves the receipt and its original expiry. At t=11 the receipt expires. At t=12 the queued retry is processed: no valid receipt exists, so the ordinary atomic implementation commits another effect and a new receipt, giving C=2. Every send respected S, operation identity remained stable, and each individual effect-plus-receipt commit was atomic. The missing protection is against processing after the original receipt expires.

reasoning_steps.title: State and prove the expiry-coverage safety condition
reasoning_steps.argument: A sufficient condition is: after the first commitment at c, every later attempt either processes while its original receipt remains valid, or is forbidden from creating an effect. To prove safety, suppose a first duplicate occurs at p. If p<c+T, the original receipt is still valid and the atomic replay rule forbids an effect, a contradiction. If p>=c+T, the additional condition forbids an effect, also a contradiction. Crashes expose neither split durable states nor a bypass of the checks. Thus every finite execution prefix has C<=1, and an infinite execution cannot have a violation without a finite first violation. The old equivalence 'receipt present iff C=1' must be dropped: after expiry C=1 with no valid receipt is allowed. The replacement invariant is C<=1 together with the requirement that an expired, previously committed operation cannot again be effect-eligible. This requirement must be enforced by a concrete contract, not inferred from the client's uncertainty.

reasoning_steps.title: Sufficient contract A: bound the last possible processing
reasoning_steps.argument: Let a be a known service-clock lower bound on any first commitment, established before sending. Suppose all original requests, retries, and automatically redelivered copies are sent by service-clock time S. Further require that each copy either is permanently discarded or has its final effect-capable processing transition no later than its send time plus Δ. This bound includes transport, queues, outages, restart, and processing stalls—not just network arrival. Then L=S+Δ bounds the last possible effect-capable processing time. Require L<a+T, with strict inequality because processing at expiry is unsafe in the ordinary service. Since a first commitment satisfies c>=a, L<a+T<=c+T; every later possible execution therefore occurs before receipt expiry and is deduplicated. This proves at-most-once safety under the stated processing bound. If a client's cutoff clock has a known upper conversion error ε, replace S by S_client+ε. Without a finite Δ or an equivalent discard rule, a send cutoff does not bound L, and the preceding duplication trace applies. A restarted client that resets S also violates this contract.

reasoning_steps.title: Sufficient contract B: service-enforced rejection without a delay bound
reasoning_steps.argument: Before the first send, bind k and x to an authoritative, immutable validity interval [a,D), with 0<D-a<=T. The service can validate that binding even after deleting the receipt. No recovery or credential reissue may extend D or substitute a fresh key for this logical operation. At the atomic processing transition, a valid receipt may be returned without an effect; otherwise a new effect is permitted only if a<=t<D. At t>=D the service must reject effect creation, including requests admitted or queued before D. Restart and replica failover must preserve this rule. Any first commitment has c>=a, hence its expiry e=c+T>=a+T>=D. A supposed duplicate at p<D encounters the valid original receipt because p<D<=e; at p>=D it is rejected by the execution gate. Therefore C<=1 without any delivery-delay bound. The equality D=a+T is safe because the gate rejects at D, whereas the ordinary service would allow a new effect at receipt expiry. This is a sufficient contract, not a claim that deadline tokens are the only solution; durable tombstones or other fencing protocols require their own analysis.

reasoning_steps.title: Explain completion, reporting, and safe stopping
reasoning_steps.argument: Neither sufficient contract guarantees completion. Under contract B, if every request is lost or reaches effect-capable processing only at t>=D, C remains zero even if delivery is eventually reliable. Completion requires a successful eligible commitment before D; truthful reporting additionally requires receipt delivery or another authoritative observation. If a committed receipt expires before acknowledgment, an 'expired/unknown' response must not be interpreted as proof of either failure or success. A client that stops sending has not canceled already queued requests. Under contract B, only passage of the enforced service deadline establishes that such requests cannot create later effects; before D they may still commit. Retrying after D under a new key to improve completion sacrifices this proof. Longer windows can preserve more recovery opportunities but require correspondingly longer retention under this construction; their storage, latency, and cost effects remain unmeasured. Safe escalation is a separate outcome, not verified task success.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify an expiry-boundary discriminator
reasoning_steps.argument: Proposed deterministic test, not executed: use independent cloned fixtures, integer clock ticks, a=c=1, T=10, e=D=11, one initial committed effect, lost acknowledgment, stable-key recovery, and a retry sent at t=2. Process the retry at p=10,11,12 in separate fixtures. Ordinary finite retention predicts final C values 1,2,2, with a cached response only at p=10. The service-deadline contract predicts 1,1,1, with cached success at p=10 and expired/unknown rejection at p=11 and p=12. In matched zero-initial-effect controls, ordinary retention predicts C=1 at each processing time; the deadline contract predicts 1,0,0. These controls distinguish genuine rejection from a test harness that never executes retries. Include gateway admission before D followed by processing after D: an ingress-only deadline check must not count as compliant. Repeat with restart spanning expiry, a deliberately rolled-back clock as a negative control, and multiple queued copies. An independent append-only audit ledger should count actual effects by logical operation identity, not by retry key or receipt existence. Record processing time, gate decision, expiry, effect count, response truthfulness, attempts, and recovery outcome. For contract A, classify any processing after L as a violated premise, not a counterexample to its conditional theorem.

reasoning_steps.argument: The evidence table currently has three analytical entries: ordinary A/K with finite retention admits the constructed duplicate; A/K plus a bounded-processing contract prevents duplication under its strong timing premise; A/K plus a persistent service execution gate prevents duplication under unbounded request delay but can reject an operation that never committed. No entry has an implemented mechanism, measured effect size, audited real-tool contract, or cost estimate. This advances the retention/expiry component of the contract-validation obligation and supplies a discriminating experiment, but does not resolve that empirical obligation, concurrency beyond the serialized model, durable repair, multi-service correctness, or delayed harm. The argument uses standard state-machine safety reasoning; material novelty and empirical generality are not assessed without source access and experiments.

reasoning_steps.title: 1. Define the operation and the safety boundary
reasoning_steps.argument: Fix one logical operation o with immutable payload p and stable key k, initially unperformed. All retries, restored agents, queues, and repair workers preserve this identity. Let N count its actual irreversible effects, across all execution paths. Its durable service state S is PENDING, APPLIED, or CANCELLED. PENDING means no effect has committed, not merely that a client lacks an acknowledgment. The modeled effect is the actual durable outcome, not an outbox insertion or dispatch intention. Actions outside this boundary and downstream delayed harms are not covered.

reasoning_steps.title: 2. State the crash and concurrency contract
reasoning_steps.argument: For k, state tests, terminal decisions, and the actual effect have a linearizable order consistent with completed calls. The effect and APPLIED record commit indivisibly and durably. Cancellation commits CANCELLED durably before its success response is sent. Crashes and failover preserve committed terminal states; an interrupted transition has either no durable outcome or its complete durable outcome. Every effect-capable path must use this same gate at commitment: an earlier read of PENDING is never a transferable execution authorization. Terminal states are not reset or deleted in the baseline contract.

reasoning_steps.title: 3. Specify the complete transition and response table
reasoning_steps.argument: For a matching key and payload: from PENDING, Execute atomically performs one effect and sets APPLIED, returning APPLIED only after durable commitment; Cancel atomically sets CANCELLED without an effect, returning CANCELLED only after durable commitment. From APPLIED, Execute replays APPLIED without another effect, and Cancel returns ALREADY_APPLIED without changing state. From CANCELLED, both Execute and Cancel return CANCELLED without an effect. Status returns the authoritative state but does not turn PENDING into a cancellation decision. Payload conflicts and invalid authorization return errors without effects. A timeout or disconnected call has outcome UNKNOWN to the caller, not CANCELLED.

reasoning_steps.title: 4. Handle cancellation before execution registration
reasoning_steps.argument: The main theorem starts with a durable PENDING record and a client mapping to k established before any send. To support reordered cancellation arriving before registration, initialization must also be atomic: an authorized Cancel on an absent k installs a bound CANCELLED tombstone; registration and execution must never overwrite it. Equivalently, absent-key cancellation may return UNKNOWN or NOT_REGISTERED without the strong guarantee. Returning CANCELLED for an absent key without installing suppression is unsafe: the delayed original registration can subsequently create PENDING and execute. Keys cannot be reused, and the operation binding must be checked.

reasoning_steps.title: 5. Prove the invariant
reasoning_steps.argument: The invariant is (S=PENDING implies N=0), (S=CANCELLED implies N=0), and (S=APPLIED implies N=1). Initially S=PENDING and N=0. The only effect-producing transition changes (PENDING,0) to (APPLIED,1) atomically. Cancellation changes (PENDING,0) to (CANCELLED,0). All terminal-state calls, status observations, errors, and queue operations leave S and N unchanged. A crash preserves the preceding committed state or the full next state, so it also preserves the invariant. These cases exhaust the stipulated transitions; induction proves the invariant for every finite history prefix, with any number of workers or crashes. Atomic absent-key cancellation, if supported, initializes (CANCELLED,0) and preserves the same argument.

reasoning_steps.title: 6. Enumerate effect–cancellation races
reasoning_steps.argument: Starting in PENDING, exactly three classes of committed outcome exist. Cancel wins first: S=CANCELLED, N=0; every subsequent Execute is suppressed. Execute wins first: S=APPLIED, N=1; cancellation returns ALREADY_APPLIED. Neither commits: S=PENDING, N=0; neither outcome has been established and a later transition may win. Concurrent calls reduce to these classes by linearizability. A cancellation request sent earlier can lose if its transition commits later; request time, queue order, and a worker's earlier PENDING read do not determine the winner. Multiple cancellations replay CANCELLED; multiple executions cannot add effects after the first APPLIED commit.

reasoning_steps.title: 7. Enumerate crash and acknowledgment boundaries
reasoning_steps.argument: Crash before a terminal commit: the durable state remains PENDING, unless the competing call commits; retry or lookup must discover the eventual winner. Crash during either atomic transition: recovery exposes only its precommit or complete postcommit state, never an effect with PENDING or CANCELLED. Cancel commits, then crash or response loss: CANCELLED persists, N=0, and retry returns CANCELLED. Execute commits, then crash or response loss: APPLIED persists, N=1, Execute replays APPLIED and Cancel returns ALREADY_APPLIED. Response received, then client crashes before checkpointing it: the service terminal state still persists; restored clients reuse k and recover the same classification. Lost responses create uncertainty, not permission to report cancellation. These cases cover each transition's before, during, after-commit/before-response, and after-response/client-persistence boundaries; further crashes repeat the same cases.

reasoning_steps.title: 8. Prove what a CANCELLED acknowledgment establishes
reasoning_steps.argument: A valid CANCELLED response is sent only after committing or authoritatively observing S=CANCELLED. The invariant then gives N=0. CANCELLED is absorbing, and the only effect transition requires PENDING, so no later transition can increase N. Every finite later prefix therefore still has N=0, excluding an effect at any later event, including execution by a queued, overlapping, resumed, or repair worker that obeys the gate. By contrast, ALREADY_APPLIED implies S=APPLIED and N=1: cancellation lost and cannot undo the irreversible effect. The contract guarantees no additional execution in that state, but does not certify that the existing effect was desired or harmless.

reasoning_steps.title: 9. Exhibit failures of stopping and unfenced acknowledgments
reasoning_steps.argument: Client-stop trace: a request is queued while S=PENDING; the client stops; the service later commits Execute, giving N=1. Thus stopping alone excludes no later effect. Unfenced-check trace: worker W reads PENDING and pauses; Cancel writes CANCELLED and acknowledges; W resumes and performs an effect without an atomic current-state test. This produces N=1 after the acknowledgment. Premature-response trace: Cancel acknowledges before durable commitment, crashes and loses its cancellation write; a surviving request executes. A transaction covering only cancellation metadata and an outbox does not eliminate either problem if the downstream actual effect remains independently executable. These are constructed counterexamples to weakened contracts, not observed failure rates.

reasoning_steps.title: 10. Derive cancellation-tombstone retention requirements
reasoning_steps.argument: Suppose cancellation commits at x, its tombstone is deleted at d, and absence again permits registration or execution. A request held until after d can then recreate PENDING and execute. Hence no fixed finite TTL alone establishes perpetual exclusion when executable requests may survive arbitrarily long. Sufficient alternatives are: retain the bound CANCELLED suppression indefinitely; replace it atomically with equally durable rejection metadata checked by every effect path; or prove that no path can execute after a finite horizon L and retain suppression through every possible execution time. If execution is possible at L and availability is [x,d), d>L is a sufficient boundary rule. Another sufficient rule is an immutable, nonrenewable operation deadline D, enforced at the actual effect transition, with suppression retained until d>=D and execution forbidden for t>=D. The deadline must remain verifiable after deletion and across restart. Client retry cutoffs, average latency, and a timeout do not establish these premises. Removing bulky response data is permissible if the terminal rejection and operation binding remain. Preserving CANCELLED versus ALREADY_APPLIED classification for arbitrarily late queries additionally requires retained outcome evidence or an honest UNKNOWN response after evidence expires.

Eventual discovery additionally needs service progress, delivery of a retry or lookup, and durable client recording; a bound by H needs explicit timing bounds. Every effect-producing path uses this same identity and authorization. Let C count all actual irreversible effects for this operation, including effects under any erroneously substituted key. An effect committed at service time c creates a receipt valid on [c,c+T); replay does not extend expiry. Safety means C<=1 for every execution prefix, including after D and an evaluation deadline H. reasoning_steps.title: 2. Cached deduplication admits duplication even before expiry
reasoning_steps.argument: Set a=0, D=T=10. At t=1, workers W1 and W2 independently read 'no receipt' and 'eligible', then pause. At t=2, W1 commits an actual effect and its receipt, giving C=1. At t=3, W2 uses its cached absence decision and unconditionally commits another effect plus replacement receipt, giving C=2. Each effect may be atomic with its own receipt write; what is missing is a current-state conditional decision encompassing that effect. A true atomic absent-key conditional commit would reject or replay W2, so this trace refutes the specified cached-absence implementation, not every implementation that performs preliminary reads.

reasoning_steps.title: 3. Cached deadline authorization admits duplication after legitimate GC
reasoning_steps.argument: Again set a=0, D=T=10. At t=1, W2 caches authorization to execute, but stalls before its authoritative receipt lookup. W1 commits at c=2, giving C=1 and receipt expiry 12; its acknowledgment is lost. At t=12, GC legitimately deletes that expired receipt. At t=13, W2 atomically checks the current receipt state, finds it absent, and commits another effect plus receipt using its cached authorization: C=2. Thus even a current absent-receipt conditional commit is insufficient if deadline authorization can survive beyond D. This trace violates execution-time authorization, not the strengthened contract proposed below.

reasoning_steps.title: 4. Specify the sufficient effect-capable transition
reasoning_steps.argument: B_concurrent requires a per-operation linearizable transition shared by all workers and effect-producing paths. At that transition's actual commitment time t: (i) validate the immutable binding of operation, k, p, a, D, and T, rejecting mismatches; (ii) inspect the current authoritative receipt and its original expiry; (iii) if a matching unexpired committed receipt exists, return that result without an effect; (iv) otherwise, if t is outside [a,D), return NOT_ELIGIBLE_OUTCOME_UNKNOWN without an effect; (v) otherwise atomically commit exactly one actual effect and its matching committed receipt with c=t and expiry c+T. Only branch (v) creates effects. Its eligibility test and absent-valid-receipt test are inseparable from the actual effect and receipt commit. Preliminary reads are advisory, never transferable execution permission. A committed receipt may be replayed after D while still valid, because replay creates no effect.

reasoning_steps.title: 5. Cover expiry, GC, crashes, and physical commitment
reasoning_steps.argument: Receipt lookup, effect commitment, and GC have one consistent per-operation order. Logical expiry is determined by current authoritative time, independently of whether physical deletion has occurred. GC may remove only the currently identified receipt version when t>=c+T; it cannot delete an unexpired receipt, erase authorization enforcement, or install reusable permission. Service time is coherent and nondecreasing across workers, restarts, and failover, and advances through outages. Crashes expose either the entire effect-plus-receipt commit or neither; unexpired receipts survive. Authorization remains verifiable after receipt deletion and cannot be renewed for this operation. Critically, t is the actual irreversible effect commitment time, not ingress time, transaction-start time, or an earlier chosen linearization timestamp. Committing a local intent before D and executing an unguarded downstream effect later does not satisfy this contract.

reasoning_steps.title: 6. Establish retention coverage of the entire eligibility interval
reasoning_steps.argument: If a first effect commits at c, branch (v) implies a<=c<D. Its receipt expires at e=c+T. Since c>=a and T>=D-a, e=c+T>=a+T>=D. Therefore, after the first effect and at every later eligible time t<D, t<e: the first receipt is still valid and cannot legitimately be removed by GC. The equality case e=D is safe because eligibility is strictly t<D and receipt validity is strictly t<e. This is a deduction from the contract, not a claim about any deployed retention guarantee.

reasoning_steps.argument: Initially C=0. Replay, rejection, GC, and crashes cannot increment C. Suppose a first effect commits at c and consider any purported next effect-producing transition at t, ordered after it. If t<D, the retention lemma guarantees the first receipt is present and valid, so the transition must replay rather than create an effect. If t>=D, current eligibility forbids creation even if the receipt has expired or been deleted. Times below a also forbid creation. These cases exhaust all times, contradicting a second effect. Concurrent attempts with equal clock values are still ordered by the atomic per-operation transition: the second observes the first receipt. Crashes preserve the relevant committed state by assumption. reasoning_steps.title: Separate the current measurement question from incomplete historical evidence
reasoning_steps.argument: The supplied extract of fdfb1b57-9f8a-451c-b9b4-2cca9cbf618f concerns ambiguous external writes, not statistical audit coverage. Its correction is concrete: if all retries are dropped, issuing a retry need not duplicate an already committed operation; therefore the inequality Pr(success|W1) <= 1-q cannot be retained without the retry-commitment premise or a newly justified replacement. I reject that relaxation and leave its crash-boundary extension unresolved. I adopt only the measurement lesson that an agent's local completion report does not determine actual external-state correctness. The statistical artifacts referenced by the ledger are not supplied originals, so no historical bound is assumed here.

reasoning_steps.title: Define a finite, realized target rather than an unobserved deployment population
reasoning_steps.argument: Freeze M >= 1 scheduled pairs after execution and before drawing the audit. For pair i, let Y_Ai and Y_Bi be binary satisfaction of a prespecified actual-outcome rubric at a fixed horizon, including required external effects and reporting correctness. Define G_i = 1{Y_Ai=1,Y_Bi=0}, L_i = 1{Y_Ai=0,Y_Bi=1}, G = sum_i G_i, and L = sum_i L_i. The target is Delta_panel = M^(-1) sum_i(Y_Ai-Y_Bi) = (G-L)/M. All execution outcomes may be dependent. This is a descriptive paired contrast; without controlled assignment it is not a causal effect. Unexecuted scheduled slots must have a prespecified operational score, such as incomplete, rather than being silently removed or treated as observed hypothetical executions.

reasoning_steps.title: Use audit randomness, not execution independence
reasoning_steps.argument: Independently of the frozen outcomes, draw an m-element subset uniformly without replacement from the M pairs, where 1 <= m <= M. If the audited gains and losses were fully known, their counts X_G and X_L would each have a hypergeometric marginal distribution: Pr_K(X=x) = binom(K,x) binom(M-K,m-x) / binom(M,m), with K respectively G or L and out-of-range binomial coefficients zero. This follows by counting subsets containing x of the K marked pairs. It requires no independence between X_G and X_L, nor between any agent executions.

reasoning_steps.title: Construct exact directional count bounds
reasoning_steps.argument: Fix 0 < alpha < 1 and a = alpha/2. Write T_K(x) = Pr_K(X >= x) and F_K(x) = Pr_K(X <= x). Define ell(x) = min{K in {0,...,M}: T_K(x) > a} and u(x) = max{K in {0,...,M}: F_K(x) > a}. These sets are nonempty: K=M makes the upper-tail probability one, and K=0 makes the lower-tail probability one for any 0 <= x <= m. Coupling populations by adding marked items shows X is stochastically increasing in K; therefore T_K increases and F_K decreases with K. Both ell and u are nondecreasing functions of the observed count.

reasoning_steps.title: Prove marginal coverage and combine it without assuming independent labels
reasoning_steps.argument: For true K, ell(X)>K implies T_K(X)<=a. Because T_K(x) decreases in x, the event T_K(X)<=a is an upper-tail event whose probability is at most a: if its smallest attainable count is c, its probability is T_K(c)<=a; if no such count exists it is zero. Likewise, u(X)<K implies F_K(X)<=a, a lower-tail event of probability at most a. Consequently Pr(ell(X_G)<=G) >= 1-a and Pr(L<=u(X_L)) >= 1-a. The union bound gives simultaneous validity at least 1-alpha, regardless of dependence between these events. On this event, Delta_panel >= [ell(X_G)-u(X_L)]/M.

reasoning_steps.title: Handle missing or disputed audit labels by sound sets of possible outcomes
reasoning_steps.argument: For each audited pair, record a nonempty set C_i contained in {00,01,10,11} that contains its actual outcome, with coordinates ordered A,B. A certified gain requires C_i={10}; a possible loss means 01 belongs to C_i. Let g_cert count certified gains and l_pos count possible losses. Pointwise, g_cert<=X_G and l_pos>=X_L. Monotonicity then gives ell(g_cert)<=ell(X_G) and u(l_pos)>=u(X_L). Thus the reported lower bound B = [ell(g_cert)-u(l_pos)]/M is no larger than the fully labeled bound and retains coverage at least 1-alpha. This remains true even if which labels become unresolved depends on outcomes or on the chosen audit subset. Completely missing evidence receives C_i={00,01,10,11}; missing labels are not dropped. The essential premise is containment of the actual outcome, not the confidence or agreement of adjudicators.

reasoning_steps.title: Check census and no-information edge cases
reasoning_steps.argument: If m=M, the hypergeometric sample count equals K deterministically, giving ell(x)=u(x)=x. With fully resolved labels, B equals Delta_panel exactly. With unresolved labels, the census bound becomes (g_cert-l_pos)/M, the minimum compatible contrast: choose outcome 01 wherever it remains possible, choose a nongain elsewhere unless 10 is forced. If every audited pair is completely unresolved, g_cert=0 and l_pos=m, so ell(0)=0, u(m)=M, and B=-1. The procedure therefore does not manufacture positive evidence from missing or ungrounded labels.

reasoning_steps.title: Identify what this certificate cannot establish
reasoning_steps.argument: A positive B supports only that A's realized panel success rate exceeds B's at confidence at least 1-alpha over the randomized audit. It does not show that the panel represents deployment tasks, that future executions have the same distribution, that A caused an improvement, or that a binary rubric captures delayed harm. Audit randomization also cannot repair unsound outcome sets: without any connection to actual outcomes, the same observed reports can accompany all pairs being 10 or all pairs being 01, yielding contrasts +1 and -1. Independent state inspection or another justified outcome constraint is therefore necessary for a nontrivial actual-correctness claim. Execution-cluster independence is avoided for this finite-panel target, not established for any population target.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify the bounded discriminating test and practical reporting protocol
reasoning_steps.argument: When execution becomes available, enumerate all outcome rosters for M<=6 and all audit subsets for each m, compute B from exact hypergeometric probabilities, and verify that the fraction of subsets with B>Delta_panel is at most alpha. Include perfectly correlated outcomes, all-gain/all-loss controls, a census, and outcome-dependent label masking; verify masking never increases B. For an applied pilot, freeze versions, prompts, budgets, pair roster, rubric, horizon, audit size, and random seed before inspection; draw the audit only after the panel is frozen. Use an instrumented append service with an independently retained operation ledger to distinguish absent, single, and duplicate effects, retaining ambiguous cases as outcome sets. Report B, unresolved-label counts, omissions, severity categories, and total execution-plus-audit costs. This is a proposed test, not measured coverage or an engineering-benefit result.

These are premises of the explicitly conditional claim. For binary paired outcomes, Y_Ai-Y_Bi equals G_i-L_i pointwise, giving the stated descriptive contrast. Prespecified nonexecution scoring avoids silently changing the denominator.

Conditional on any fixed roster, counting uniformly selected subsets gives the displayed hypergeometric mass function. Neither independence among executions nor independence of gain and loss counts is used.

The endpoint populations ensure nonempty inversion sets. Coupling nested marked populations proves stochastic ordering in K. Increasing the observed count makes the lower-bound threshold no smaller and the upper-bound admissible set no larger at its lower end, yielding nondecreasing ell and u.

Each inversion failure implies a corresponding discrete tail probability at most a. Such a tail event has probability at most a under the true K. Applying the union bound to the gain-lower and loss-upper events establishes the contrast bound without joint independence.

Under actual-outcome containment, every certified gain is real and every real audited loss is possible. The resulting pointwise count inequalities and monotone inversion functions make the conservative bound no larger than the fully labeled bound, even under outcome-dependent masking.

A census makes the hypergeometric count deterministic and both inversions equal the observed count. Minimizing each unresolved pair's contrast gives a loss whenever possible, a gain only when forced, and zero otherwise. Completely unrestricted labels therefore produce the lower bound -1.

The coverage proof is conditional on the realized roster and audit mechanism, so it provides neither population transport nor causality. Identical unconstrained reports can accompany opposite true rosters, demonstrating why outcome constraints remain necessary.

Enumeration would directly test an implementation's finite-roster coverage, and masking monotonicity is an appropriate control. The pilot and reporting requirements are useful proposals, explicitly not completed experiments. Audit randomization must operationally remain independent of the sealed outcomes.
