reasoning_steps.title: Separate the current measurement question from incomplete historical evidence
reasoning_steps.argument: The supplied extract of fdfb1b57-9f8a-451c-b9b4-2cca9cbf618f concerns ambiguous external writes, not statistical audit coverage. Its correction is concrete: if all retries are dropped, issuing a retry need not duplicate an already committed operation; therefore the inequality Pr(success|W1) <= 1-q cannot be retained without the retry-commitment premise or a newly justified replacement. I reject that relaxation and leave its crash-boundary extension unresolved. I adopt only the measurement lesson that an agent's local completion report does not determine actual external-state correctness. The statistical artifacts referenced by the ledger are not supplied originals, so no historical bound is assumed here.

review.rationale: The supplied extract explicitly contains the dropped-retry counterexample: issuing a retry need not create another effect. Rejecting that relaxation while avoiding reliance on unavailable statistical originals is justified.

reasoning_steps.title: Define a finite, realized target rather than an unobserved deployment population
reasoning_steps.argument: Freeze M >= 1 scheduled pairs after execution and before drawing the audit. For pair i, let Y_Ai and Y_Bi be binary satisfaction of a prespecified actual-outcome rubric at a fixed horizon, including required external effects and reporting correctness. Define G_i = 1{Y_Ai=1,Y_Bi=0}, L_i = 1{Y_Ai=0,Y_Bi=1}, G = sum_i G_i, and L = sum_i L_i. The target is Delta_panel = M^(-1) sum_i(Y_Ai-Y_Bi) = (G-L)/M. All execution outcomes may be dependent. This is a descriptive paired contrast; without controlled assignment it is not a causal effect. Unexecuted scheduled slots must have a prespecified operational score, such as incomplete, rather than being silently removed or treated as observed hypothetical executions.

review.rationale: These are premises of the explicitly conditional claim. For binary paired outcomes, Y_Ai-Y_Bi equals G_i-L_i pointwise, giving the stated descriptive contrast. Prespecified nonexecution scoring avoids silently changing the denominator.

reasoning_steps.title: Use audit randomness, not execution independence
reasoning_steps.argument: Independently of the frozen outcomes, draw an m-element subset uniformly without replacement from the M pairs, where 1 <= m <= M. If the audited gains and losses were fully known, their counts X_G and X_L would each have a hypergeometric marginal distribution: Pr_K(X=x) = binom(K,x) binom(M-K,m-x) / binom(M,m), with K respectively G or L and out-of-range binomial coefficients zero. This follows by counting subsets containing x of the K marked pairs. It requires no independence between X_G and X_L, nor between any agent executions.

review.rationale: Conditional on any fixed roster, counting uniformly selected subsets gives the displayed hypergeometric mass function. Neither independence among executions nor independence of gain and loss counts is used.

reasoning_steps.title: Construct exact directional count bounds
reasoning_steps.argument: Fix 0 < alpha < 1 and a = alpha/2. Write T_K(x) = Pr_K(X >= x) and F_K(x) = Pr_K(X <= x). Define ell(x) = min{K in {0,...,M}: T_K(x) > a} and u(x) = max{K in {0,...,M}: F_K(x) > a}. These sets are nonempty: K=M makes the upper-tail probability one, and K=0 makes the lower-tail probability one for any 0 <= x <= m. Coupling populations by adding marked items shows X is stochastically increasing in K; therefore T_K increases and F_K decreases with K. Both ell and u are nondecreasing functions of the observed count.

review.rationale: The endpoint populations ensure nonempty inversion sets. Coupling nested marked populations proves stochastic ordering in K. Increasing the observed count makes the lower-bound threshold no smaller and the upper-bound admissible set no larger at its lower end, yielding nondecreasing ell and u.

reasoning_steps.title: Prove marginal coverage and combine it without assuming independent labels
reasoning_steps.argument: For true K, ell(X)>K implies T_K(X)<=a. Because T_K(x) decreases in x, the event T_K(X)<=a is an upper-tail event whose probability is at most a: if its smallest attainable count is c, its probability is T_K(c)<=a; if no such count exists it is zero. Likewise, u(X)<K implies F_K(X)<=a, a lower-tail event of probability at most a. Consequently Pr(ell(X_G)<=G) >= 1-a and Pr(L<=u(X_L)) >= 1-a. The union bound gives simultaneous validity at least 1-alpha, regardless of dependence between these events. On this event, Delta_panel >= [ell(X_G)-u(X_L)]/M.

review.rationale: Each inversion failure implies a corresponding discrete tail probability at most a. Such a tail event has probability at most a under the true K. Applying the union bound to the gain-lower and loss-upper events establishes the contrast bound without joint independence.

reasoning_steps.title: Handle missing or disputed audit labels by sound sets of possible outcomes
reasoning_steps.argument: For each audited pair, record a nonempty set C_i contained in {00,01,10,11} that contains its actual outcome, with coordinates ordered A,B. A certified gain requires C_i={10}; a possible loss means 01 belongs to C_i. Let g_cert count certified gains and l_pos count possible losses. Pointwise, g_cert<=X_G and l_pos>=X_L. Monotonicity then gives ell(g_cert)<=ell(X_G) and u(l_pos)>=u(X_L). Thus the reported lower bound B = [ell(g_cert)-u(l_pos)]/M is no larger than the fully labeled bound and retains coverage at least 1-alpha. This remains true even if which labels become unresolved depends on outcomes or on the chosen audit subset. Completely missing evidence receives C_i={00,01,10,11}; missing labels are not dropped. The essential premise is containment of the actual outcome, not the confidence or agreement of adjudicators.

review.rationale: Under actual-outcome containment, every certified gain is real and every real audited loss is possible. The resulting pointwise count inequalities and monotone inversion functions make the conservative bound no larger than the fully labeled bound, even under outcome-dependent masking.

reasoning_steps.title: Check census and no-information edge cases
reasoning_steps.argument: If m=M, the hypergeometric sample count equals K deterministically, giving ell(x)=u(x)=x. With fully resolved labels, B equals Delta_panel exactly. With unresolved labels, the census bound becomes (g_cert-l_pos)/M, the minimum compatible contrast: choose outcome 01 wherever it remains possible, choose a nongain elsewhere unless 10 is forced. If every audited pair is completely unresolved, g_cert=0 and l_pos=m, so ell(0)=0, u(m)=M, and B=-1. The procedure therefore does not manufacture positive evidence from missing or ungrounded labels.

review.rationale: A census makes the hypergeometric count deterministic and both inversions equal the observed count. Minimizing each unresolved pair's contrast gives a loss whenever possible, a gain only when forced, and zero otherwise. Completely unrestricted labels therefore produce the lower bound -1.

reasoning_steps.title: Identify what this certificate cannot establish
reasoning_steps.argument: A positive B supports only that A's realized panel success rate exceeds B's at confidence at least 1-alpha over the randomized audit. It does not show that the panel represents deployment tasks, that future executions have the same distribution, that A caused an improvement, or that a binary rubric captures delayed harm. Audit randomization also cannot repair unsound outcome sets: without any connection to actual outcomes, the same observed reports can accompany all pairs being 10 or all pairs being 01, yielding contrasts +1 and -1. Independent state inspection or another justified outcome constraint is therefore necessary for a nontrivial actual-correctness claim. Execution-cluster independence is avoided for this finite-panel target, not established for any population target.

review.rationale: The coverage proof is conditional on the realized roster and audit mechanism, so it provides neither population transport nor causality. Identical unconstrained reports can accompany opposite true rosters, demonstrating why outcome constraints remain necessary.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify the bounded discriminating test and practical reporting protocol
reasoning_steps.argument: When execution becomes available, enumerate all outcome rosters for M<=6 and all audit subsets for each m, compute B from exact hypergeometric probabilities, and verify that the fraction of subsets with B>Delta_panel is at most alpha. Include perfectly correlated outcomes, all-gain/all-loss controls, a census, and outcome-dependent label masking; verify masking never increases B. For an applied pilot, freeze versions, prompts, budgets, pair roster, rubric, horizon, audit size, and random seed before inspection; draw the audit only after the panel is frozen. Use an instrumented append service with an independently retained operation ledger to distinguish absent, single, and duplicate effects, retaining ambiguous cases as outcome sets. Report B, unresolved-label counts, omissions, severity categories, and total execution-plus-audit costs. This is a proposed test, not measured coverage or an engineering-benefit result.

review.rationale: Enumeration would directly test an implementation's finite-roster coverage, and masking monotonicity is an appropriate control. The pilot and reporting requirements are useful proposals, explicitly not completed experiments. Audit randomization must operationally remain independent of the sealed outcomes.

objective_review.claim: Conditional on: A finite roster of M paired execution slots, their actual binary rubric outcomes, and the observation horizon are fixed before audit selection; audit inspection does not change those outcomes; Every scheduled slot remains in the denominator, with prespecified operational treatment of nonexecution; the claim does not concern hypothetical outcomes of omitted executions; The m audited pairs form a uniformly random subset without replacement, independent of the frozen outcomes, with 1 <= m <= M; Every audited possible-outcome set contains the actual pair outcome. A disputed or unavailable label is represented conservatively rather than assumed correct; The confidence level satisfies 0 < alpha < 1 and is fixed before inspecting audit outcomes. Conditional on the Investigator's five listed assumptions, uniform post-execution auditing of a frozen paired roster yields a one-sided confidence bound on its actual success-rate difference, without execution-outcome independence, and conservative sound outcome sets preserve coverage.
objective_review.argument_summary: For fixed gain and loss totals G and L, uniform sampling without replacement gives hypergeometric marginal audit counts. Directional tail inversion bounds G below and L above, each with error at most alpha/2. Their simultaneous event has probability at least 1-alpha by the union bound. Certified gains undercount true audited gains, and possible losses overcount true audited losses; monotonicity therefore preserves coverage of the lower contrast bound. Census and completely unresolved-label limits behave correctly. The result is descriptive and roster-specific.

artifacts.strategy_title: Understand failure propagation and recovery in autonomous AI agents
artifacts.claim_or_question: Conditional recovery result: for one logical operation, a durable stable key plus a serializable, atomic effect-and-completion-record transaction prevents duplicate effects; eventual request processing and response delivery additionally give eventual verified completion, but not completion by a fixed deadline H. Stable keys alone do not suffice when effect and completion-record writes are non-atomic. Regenerating keys after ambiguous outcomes defeats even the atomic implementation. The six-case crash analysis below establishes these statements within an explicit service model, not for deployed tools.
artifacts.method: Correct the supplied prior argument's delivery-relaxation error, then derive crash-prefix transitions for three service implementations crossed with stable versus regenerated keys. Hypothesis: both key continuity and atomic coupling of the actual effect to its completion record are needed for the stated recovery guarantee. The discriminator is independently audited external-effect count and receipt validity after recovery, not the agent's completion claim. Hold payload, logical operation, initial state, retry schedule, and crash position fixed across implementations; use no-crash and no-retry controls. The transition analysis is analytical, not an executed experiment. Both runtimes are unavailable, so no computation is requested. Recorded timeout/cancellation failures motivate a bounded standalone analysis, not repetition of an unavailable execution. Operational failures are not mathematical evidence.
assumptions: One logical operation has a fixed payload and initially no effect; effects are irreversible and non-idempotent, and C counts all its effects across keys.
The atomic implementation couples the actual durable effect and its terminal completion record in one serializable transaction; crashes cannot expose a partial durable commit.
Completion records survive crashes, remain available for every possible retry, validate payload identity, and suppress repeated execution for their key. Keys are not reused for unrelated operations.
The stable policy durably records the operation-to-key-and-payload mapping before sending and never replaces that key while recovering the operation.

The non-atomic implementations treat D as terminal completion; interrupted handlers are abandoned and no background repair fills missing effects or records. The counterexample traces use serialized requests.

The crash table assumes one subsequent retry is processed without another crash. The general eventual-completion result instead requires continued pending retries, eventual successful service processing and response delivery, and durable local completion.
No bounded response or recovery time is assumed. A guarantee by H requires an additional explicit timing premise.
artifacts.evidence_status: Conditional analytical derivation and constructed traces only; no executed fault injection, inspected real-service contract, external literature access, or independent verification. The supplied prior extract supports identifying the delivery-relaxation objection, not certifying its unavailable original. These are standard transaction and retry principles; material novelty and deployment generality are not assessed. The contribution is a six-case falsifiable recovery specification and separation
artifacts.skeptic_response:
The current analytical result is convincing within its stated model. The delivery-relaxation error identified in the supplied extract of fdfb1b57-9f8a-451c-b9b4-2cca9cbf618f is correctly withdrawn locally. All six crash cases follow from the specified durable writes, terminal-record semantics, abandoned handlers, and one crash-free retry. The atomic/stable-key invariant establishes at-most-once effects; eventual processing, response delivery, and durable client completion supply the separate liveness conditions. Neither establishes completion by H without timing bounds.

This completes a useful local derivation, not the project's empirical objective. There is no execution record, real-service audit, measured recovery benefit, or independent verification. Both runtimes are unavailable; provider failures are operational history, not evidence about the claim. Rather than repeat an unavailable experiment, a concrete next step is to examine finite deduplication retention and delayed requests, which directly challenge the permanent-record premise.

reasoning_steps.title: Define observable success and service state
reasoning_steps.argument: Consider one initially unperformed logical operation with a fixed payload. Let C count its irreversible durable effects across all keys, and let e_k count effects under key k. Let d_k be a durable terminal completion record containing the payload and a success receipt. Initially C=e_k=d_k=0. External-state correctness at H means C(H)=1; full task completion additionally requires an accurate terminal report by H. C=0, C>=2, and escalation are separate outcomes. Each actual effect increments C and its e_k by one. A service receipt is not assumed accurate merely because it exists.

reasoning_steps.title: Define implementation and crash semantics
reasoning_steps.argument: On a request, the service checks d_k. If present with matching payload, it returns the cached receipt without executing an effect; mismatched payloads are rejected. For an absent record, A atomically commits effect E and record D; ED persists E before D; DE persists D before E. D is treated as completed, not as a pending intent. Crashes retain durable writes but discard the interrupted handler, and there is no background repair of partial ED or DE operations. Requests are serialized, so concurrency is not needed for the counterexamples. Replies normally follow the whole sequence. For the crash table, retry processing has no further crash and completes if it is not suppressed by D.

reasoning_steps.title: Define the two key policies and table interpretation
reasoning_steps.argument: Stable means the operation-to-key-and-payload mapping is durable before the first send and every retry reuses that key. Regenerated means recovery sends the same logical operation under a fresh unused key. Each table case starts from an unused key, runs the original request to a specified durable boundary, loses the reply or crashes, and then retries once. Reported counts are after that retry is handled. For A the possible boundaries are before and after its atomic commit; a crash during the transaction has one of those durable outcomes. For ED they are before E, between E and D, and after D. For DE they are before D, between D and E, and after E. A crash after reply delivery but before durable local completion produces the same retry cases if the local pending record survives.

reasoning_steps.title: Crash table: atomic service with a stable key
reasoning_steps.argument: A × stable: before commit, (e_k,d_k)=(0,0), so retry commits (1,1), yielding C=1. After commit, (1,1), so retry returns the cached receipt and leaves C=1. No durable (1,0) or (0,1) state exists. Thus every crash boundary yields one effect after a completed retry. At the client boundary, retaining and reusing the same pending key preserves this argument even when the first reply was received but local completion was not recorded.

reasoning_steps.title: Crash table: atomic service with a regenerated key

reasoning_steps.title: Crash table: effect-before-record with a stable key

reasoning_steps.title: Crash table: effect-before-record with a regenerated key

reasoning_steps.title: Crash table: record-before-effect with a stable key

If the operation remains pending, requests are retried, and eventually one transaction can finish, C eventually becomes 1. If a valid response is eventually delivered and local completion is durably recorded, the client can truthfully finish. No-crash execution is the base case; a permanently unavailable service preserves at-most-once safety but not completion. This proof requires the actual effect—not merely a dispatch intention—to participate in the atomic transaction.

review.rationale: The stated transitions preserve e_k=d_k in {0,1} by induction, and stable-key exclusivity gives C=e_k. Eventual successful processing establishes existence of one effect; response delivery and durable local recording separately establish client completion. All required progress conditions are explicit.

reasoning_steps.title: Deadline limits and a discriminating next test
reasoning_steps.argument: Eventual progress supplies no finite completion-time bound: an otherwise valid execution can delay the first successful transaction until after H, leaving C(H)=0, or delay its response until after H. Completion by H needs an additional bounded recovery-and-response guarantee; for example, if a pending operation reaches a recoverable state by t0 and guaranteed verified completion takes at most B thereafter, t0+B<=H suffices. The next proposed test enumerates the stated crash boundaries in the 3×2 design, including client crashes after receipt arrival. Audit effects in storage independently of receipt records and agent reports. Compare boundary outcomes with the derived counts, record C(H), report accuracy, pending state, retry count, latency and cost, and continue beyond H to separate lateness from permanent omission. Any duplicate in stable A, or any receipt without an effect in A, falsifies the implemented contract or the model assumptions. No such test has been executed.

review.rationale: An eventually successful execution can delay its first commit or response beyond any fixed H, so eventual progress alone supplies no deadline guarantee. The proposed independently audited boundary test targets the derived invariants and distinguishes lateness from permanent omission; it is correctly labeled unexecuted.

objective_review.claim: Conditional on: One logical operation has a fixed payload and initially no effect; effects are irreversible and non-idempotent, and C counts all its effects across keys; The atomic implementation couples the actual durable effect and its terminal completion record in one serializable transaction; crashes cannot expose a partial durable commit; Completion records survive crashes, remain available for every possible retry, validate payload identity, and suppress repeated execution for their key. Keys are not reused for unrelated operations; The stable policy durably records the operation-to-key-and-payload mapping before sending and never replaces that key while recovering the operation; The non-atomic implementations treat D as terminal completion; interrupted handlers are abandoned and no background repair fills missing effects or records. The counterexample traces use serialized requests; The crash table assumes one subsequent retry is processed without another crash. The general eventual-completion result instead requires continued pending retries, eventual successful service processing and response delivery, and durable local completion; No bounded response or recovery time is assumed. A guarantee by H requires an additional explicit timing premise. Conditional on the Investigator's explicit service, key-persistence, crash, and progress assumptions, atomic coupling of the actual effect and its durable completion record with a stable operation key prevents duplicate effects. Eventual processing, response delivery, and durable client completion additionally yield eventual truthful completion, but not a fixed-deadline guarantee. The constructed non-atomic and regenerated-key traces demonstrate failures within that model.
objective_review.argument_summary: Cycle 1 supplies the full local argument. In the listed durable-boundary order, post-retry effect counts are A/stable: 1,1; A/regenerated: 1,2; ED/stable: 1,2,1; ED/regenerated: 1,2,2; DE/stable: 1,0,1; DE/regenerated: 1,1,2. For A/stable, each request preserves e_k=d_k in {0,1}, and using only k gives C=e_k<=1. Progress and durable client completion are additional liveness premises. Arbitrarily delayed processing or responses defeat any deadline guarantee without bounded timing. The historical delivery correction uses only the explicitly supplied passage of fdfb1b57-9f8a-451c-b9b4-2cca9cbf618f; no unavailable historical proof is needed for the crash analysis.

argument_steps.title: Scope of historical evidence and correction
argument_steps.argument: The supplied extract of fdfb1b57-9f8a-451c-b9b4-2cca9cbf618f exposes a specific invalid sentence: dropping assured retry commitment does not preserve Pr(success in W1) <= 1-q, where q is retry probability. An always-retry policy whose retries all disappear has q=1, yet the already-committed history W1 retains exactly one effect. Retract that relaxation. The original conditional bound retains its original delivery premise: success in W0 requires retry, while success in W1 excludes retry when every retry commits. Nothing here establishes that the same bound holds under arbitrary relaxed delivery. The original artifact is unavailable; this correction addresses only the explicitly supplied argument and objection.

review.rationale: The supplied prior passage makes q the probability of issuing a retry, not its commitment probability. With q=1 and every retry dropped, W1 retains one effect, contradicting the claimed upper bound 1-q. Restoring assured commitment restores the stated implication that retry duplicates W1.

argument_steps.title: Define observable success and service state
argument_steps.argument: Consider one initially unperformed logical operation with a fixed payload. Let C count its irreversible durable effects across all keys, and let e_k count effects under key k. Let d_k be a durable terminal completion record containing the payload and a success receipt. Initially C=e_k=d_k=0. External-state correctness at H means C(H)=1; full task completion additionally requires an accurate terminal report by H. C=0, C>=2, and escalation are separate outcomes. Each actual effect increments C and its e_k by one. A service receipt is not assumed accurate merely because it exists.

review.rationale: These are explicit definitions and premises of the conditional claim. Counting effects across keys prevents a key change from concealing duplication, and separating external correctness from truthful reporting avoids treating a receipt as an independent oracle.

argument_steps.title: Define implementation and crash semantics
argument_steps.argument: On a request, the service checks d_k. If present with matching payload, it returns the cached receipt without executing an effect; mismatched payloads are rejected. For an absent record, A atomically commits effect E and record D; ED persists E before D; DE persists D before E. D is treated as completed, not as a pending intent. Crashes retain durable writes but discard the interrupted handler, and there is no background repair of partial ED or DE operations. Requests are serialized, so concurrency is not needed for the counterexamples. Replies normally follow the whole sequence. For the crash table, retry processing has no further crash and completes if it is not suppressed by D.

review.rationale: The implementation semantics explicitly distinguish atomic E+D, E-before-D, and D-before-E, with terminal D suppressing retries. Serialized requests and abandoned handlers make the subsequent prefix analyses well-defined. These are stipulated premises, not established properties of real services.

argument_steps.title: Define the two key policies and table interpretation
argument_steps.argument: Stable means the operation-to-key-and-payload mapping is durable before the first send and every retry reuses that key. Regenerated means recovery sends the same logical operation under a fresh unused key. Each table case starts from an unused key, runs the original request to a specified durable boundary, loses the reply or crashes, and then retries once. Reported counts are after that retry is handled. For A the possible boundaries are before and after its atomic commit; a crash during the transaction has one of those durable outcomes. For ED they are before E, between E and D, and after D. For DE they are before D, between D and E, and after E. A crash after reply delivery but before durable local completion produces the same retry cases if the local pending record survives.

review.rationale: Durable stable-key recovery and fresh-key recovery are distinct policies. The listed boundaries exhaust the durable prefixes of the stipulated sequences; atomicity excludes partial A states. A client crash before durable completion can trigger the same retry when the pending mapping survives.

argument_steps.title: Crash table: atomic service with a stable key
argument_steps.argument: A × stable: before commit, (e_k,d_k)=(0,0), so retry commits (1,1), yielding C=1. After commit, (1,1), so retry returns the cached receipt and leaves C=1. No durable (1,0) or (0,1) state exists. Thus every crash boundary yields one effect after a completed retry. At the client boundary, retaining and reusing the same pending key preserves this argument even when the first reply was received but local completion was not recorded.

review.rationale: Before the atomic commit, retry performs the sole effect; after it, the retained completion record suppresses another effect. Both cases end at C=1 under the crash-free-retry premise.

argument_steps.title: Crash table: atomic service with a regenerated key
argument_steps.argument: A × regenerated: a pre-commit crash leaves C=0, and a fresh-key retry gives C=1. A post-commit crash leaves C=1 and d_k=1, but the fresh key k' has d_k'=0; its atomic transaction increments C to 2. Concrete chain: original atomic commit → lost acknowledgment → restored pending task → new key → second atomic commit. Atomicity protects each key, not the logical operation across different keys.

review.rationale: A fresh key has no completion record even when the original key committed. Consequently a post-commit retry adds a second effect, whereas a pre-commit retry adds the first. Per-key atomicity does not imply cross-key logical-operation deduplication.

argument_steps.title: Crash table: effect-before-record with a stable key
argument_steps.argument: ED × stable: before E, retry yields C=1. Between E and D, durable state is (e_k,d_k)=(1,0); retry sees no record, executes another E, and then writes D, yielding C=2. After D, retry is suppressed and C stays 1. Consequently the boundary outcomes are 1, 2, 1. The middle trace refutes the candidate claim that stable keys and a deduplication table alone guarantee at-most-once effects.

review.rationale: The ED middle prefix durably contains an effect but no suppressing record. A stable-key retry therefore executes another effect. The outcomes 1,2,1 follow, refuting stable-key sufficiency for this non-atomic implementation.

argument_steps.title: Crash table: effect-before-record with a regenerated key
argument_steps.argument: ED × regenerated: before E, the fresh-key retry yields C=1. Between E and D, the original effect already exists and the fresh-key retry adds another, yielding C=2. After D, the original complete operation likewise does not suppress a fresh-key request, yielding C=2. The boundary outcomes are 1, 2, 2. Fixing key continuity removes the last failure but not the non-atomic middle-window failure.

review.rationale: Fresh-key retry always executes once. Adding that effect to the original prefix counts 0,1,1 gives 1,2,2. Stable keys eliminate only the completed-original/fresh-key duplication case, not the ED partial-write case.

argument_steps.title: Crash table: record-before-effect with a stable key
argument_steps.argument: DE × stable: before D, retry executes the full sequence and yields C=1. Between D and E, durable state is (e_k,d_k)=(0,1); retry returns the cached success receipt without E, leaving C=0. With no repair process, all subsequent same-key retries remain suppressed. After E, retry is suppressed and C stays 1. The boundary outcomes are 1, 0, 1. This middle trace produces a successful-looking receipt with no actual effect, demonstrating why receipt counts cannot serve as the sole correctness oracle.

review.rationale: At the DE middle prefix, D is terminal while no effect exists. Same-key retry returns its success receipt without execution, permanently leaving C=0 under the no-repair premise. This establishes the receipt-oracle failure in the constructed model.

argument_steps.title: Crash table: record-before-effect with a regenerated key
argument_steps.argument: DE × regenerated: before D, the fresh-key retry yields C=1. Between D and E, the abandoned original has no effect; the fresh-key retry yields C=1 but leaves an invalid old completion record. After E, the original effect exists and the fresh-key retry yields C=2. The boundary outcomes are 1, 1, 2. The middle outcome is externally correct only under the stipulated absence of repair or resumption of the old handler; it does not establish a generally safe recovery policy.

review.rationale: The original DE prefix has counts 0,0,1, and a fresh-key crash-free retry adds one, yielding 1,1,2. The middle result depends on abandoning the old handler; the step correctly avoids extending it to repair or resumption.

reasoning_steps.title: Scope and historical evidence
reasoning_steps.argument: The supplied extract of fdfb1b57-9f8a-451c-b9b4-2cca9cbf618f concerns the same domain: an irreversible external effect, ambiguous acknowledgment, and recovery from a pending local checkpoint. Its original is unavailable, some fields are truncated, and it contains no completed relevant computation. reasoning_steps.title: Correct the delivery relaxation
reasoning_steps.argument: Let q be the probability of issuing a retry by deadline H in two initially indistinguishable histories with respectively zero and one prior effects. Under assured retry commitment by H, external-state correctness is bounded above by q in the first history and 1-q in the second, giving worst-case failure at least 1/2. Withdraw the claim that both inequalities survive arbitrary retry loss. If the policy always retries but every retry is dropped, then q=1 while the second history still has exactly one effect: its external-state correctness probability is 1, not at most 0. This counterexample invalidates the relaxed inequality, not the original assured-delivery construction. No replacement bound for arbitrary delivery and adaptive observations is claimed here.

reasoning_steps.title: Define the service and recovery contracts
reasoning_steps.argument: Analyze one logical operation with fixed payload x, initially no effects or receipts. Let C count its irreversible durable external effects and R[k] denote a durable terminal success receipt for key k. Each individual effect and receipt write is atomic. Service attempts are serialized, and restart abandons volatile unfinished work. There is no background reconciliation, compensation, expiry, or other deduplication. An existing R[k] returns cached success without creating an effect; reuse with a different payload is rejected. Atomic implementation A commits one effect and R[k] in one indivisible durable transition. Implementation E commits the effect and then R[k]. Implementation R commits R[k] and then the effect. Responses are sent after the intended sequence, except that replay can return an existing receipt. A stable-key client durably records (k,x) before its first send and reuses it; a regenerating client uses a fresh key after ambiguous recovery. These definitions intentionally exclude stronger split-write implementations with durable repair protocols.

reasoning_steps.title: Crash-boundary transition table
reasoning_steps.argument:
Write state as (C, receipt present for the original key). B0 is before any durable transition; B1 is between split writes; B2 is after all writes but before an acknowledgment reaches the client. A has no B1. The following table describes a subsequent retry that runs to completion; K means reuse the original key and N means use a fresh key.
Implementation/key | B0 retry | B1 crash then retry | B2 acknowledgment loss then retry
A/K | (0,0) -> (1,1) | impossible boundary | (1,1) -> (1,1), cached response
A/N | (0,0) -> one effect under new key | impossible boundary | original effect plus new-key effect: C=2
E/K | (0,0) -> (1,1) | (1,0) -> (2,1): duplicate | (1,1) -> (1,1), cached response
E/N | (0,0) -> one effect under new key | original effect plus new-key effect: C=2 | original effect plus new-key effect: C=2
R/K | (0,0) -> (1,1) | (0,1) -> (0,1): cached success, omitted effect | (1,1) -> (1,1), cached response
R/N | (0,0) -> one effect under new key | old receipt remains; new-key attempt produces C=1 | original effect plus new-key effect: C=2
For N rows, the new receipt belongs to the new key; C always aggregates the same logical operation. After a received acknowledgment and durable local completion, no retry is required. A client crash before saving that completion reduces to B2.

reasoning_steps.title: Prove the atomic stable-key safety invariant
reasoning_steps.argument: For A/K define Ck as the number of effects committed with the sole operation key. Initially Ck=0 and R[k] is absent. An interrupted atomic transition leaves either that state or the committed state Ck=1 with R[k] present. From the committed state every replay only returns the receipt. No transition removes the receipt or increments Ck again. Induction over any finite sequence of attempts and crashes therefore gives Ck in {0,1} and R[k] present if and only if Ck=1. The same safety statement holds throughout an infinite execution because every violation would have a finite first occurrence. As every send for this logical operation uses k, C=Ck and duplication is impossible. Serialization is an explicit premise; a concurrent implementation must supply equivalent linearizable atomic behavior.

reasoning_steps.title: Explain why the other cells are genuine local counterexamples
reasoning_steps.argument: E/K loses the information needed to recognize an already committed effect: crash after the effect but before its receipt, followed by a complete same-key retry, creates two effects. R/K loses the work needed to justify its receipt: crash after the receipt but before the effect leaves all subsequent same-key attempts returning success with C=0. A/N preserves the per-key invariant but not a per-logical-operation invariant: commit under k, lose acknowledgment, then commit under fresh k' gives one effect per key and two effects overall. E/N and R/N also admit this last complete-commit/lost-acknowledgment trace. Thus key regeneration may repair the particular R intermediate-crash omission, but it is not a generally safe recovery rule. These traces do not refute split-write designs with additional recovery mechanisms excluded by the model, nor establish that atomicity is necessary in every possible design.

reasoning_steps.title: Separate safety, eventual completion, and deadline completion
reasoning_steps.argument: A/K's at-most-once invariant requires no delivery guarantee. To conclude eventual C=1, additionally require continued same-key attempts until completion and a delivery/service schedule under which at least one attempt completes the atomic transition. To conclude eventual truthful terminal reporting, also require an eventual receipt delivery and client progress sufficient to record and report completion. None of these eventual-progress premises bounds completion time: delaying all useful deliveries beyond any chosen finite H satisfies eventual progress but leaves C(H)=0. Hence neither by-H success nor its probability follows from the safety invariant. Conversely, R/K's intermediate-crash omission persists even with reliable later delivery, because every later request takes the cached-receipt path.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify a controlled architectural test and its oracle
reasoning_steps.argument: Implement the six cells with the same payload, client workflow, tool interface, retry budget, and durable-state instrumentation. Inject crashes before the first write, between split writes where applicable, after the final write before acknowledgment, and after acknowledgment before local completion persistence. Include no-fault controls and request-drop controls. Audit durable effect count using an independent service-side ledger keyed by logical operation identity, not merely by the client's retry key; otherwise regenerated keys can hide duplication. Record receipt state, report correctness, C(H), eventual C after a declared recovery window, silent omissions/duplicates, attempts, latency, and cost. First test the deterministic traces above; then use prespecified repeated fault schedules and held-out workflows to estimate rates. Do not pool structurally different crash boundaries as though they had equal deployment prevalence. reasoning_steps.title: Define the service and recovery contracts
reasoning_steps.argument: Analyze one logical operation with fixed payload x, initially no effects or receipts. Let C count its irreversible durable external effects and R[k] denote a durable terminal success receipt for key k. Each individual effect and receipt write is atomic. Implementation/key | B0 retry | B1 crash then retry | B2 acknowledgment loss then retry

reasoning_steps.argument: For A/K define Ck as the number of effects committed with the sole operation key. Initially Ck=0 and R[k] is absent. argument_steps.title: Separate safety, eventual completion, and deadline completion
argument_steps.argument: A/K's at-most-once invariant requires no delivery guarantee. To conclude eventual C=1, additionally require continued same-key attempts until completion and a delivery/service schedule under which at least one attempt completes the atomic transition. To conclude eventual truthful terminal reporting, also require an eventual receipt delivery and client progress sufficient to record and report completion. None of these eventual-progress premises bounds completion time: delaying all useful deliveries beyond any chosen finite H satisfies eventual progress but leaves C(H)=0. Hence neither by-H success nor its probability follows from the safety invariant. Conversely, R/K's intermediate-crash omission persists even with reliable later delivery, because every later request takes the cached-receipt path.

review.rationale: At-most-once safety needs no successful delivery. Eventual effect creation additionally needs a completing attempt, and truthful reporting needs receipt delivery and client progress. An arbitrarily long finite delay satisfies eventual progress while defeating any specified deadline. R/K cannot repair its split state because replay always takes the cached-success branch.

argument_steps.title: Specify a controlled architectural test and its oracle
argument_steps.argument: Implement the six cells with the same payload, client workflow, tool interface, retry budget, and durable-state instrumentation. Inject crashes before the first write, between split writes where applicable, after the final write before acknowledgment, and after acknowledgment before local completion persistence. Include no-fault controls and request-drop controls. Audit durable effect count using an independent service-side ledger keyed by logical operation identity, not merely by the client's retry key; otherwise regenerated keys can hide duplication. Record receipt state, report correctness, C(H), eventual C after a declared recovery window, silent omissions/duplicates, attempts, latency, and cost. First test the deterministic traces above; then use prespecified repeated fault schedules and held-out workflows to estimate rates. Do not pool structurally different crash boundaries as though they had equal deployment prevalence. For stochastic agent comparisons, randomize mechanism assignment within task/fault strata, use separate cloned environments, freeze model/prompt versions and budgets, and report task-cluster uncertainty and budget exhaustion. No such tests have been run here.

reasoning_steps.title: Define finite retention, execution and concurrency
reasoning_steps.argument: One initially unperformed logical operation has a fixed payload p and a durably assigned key k. Every execution path for it uses k; keys are not reused. C counts all actual irreversible effects for the operation. A successful first execution at service time c atomically increments C and creates completion record D(k,p). Under the expiry-only implementation, D suppresses effects during [c,c+T), where T>0, and may be deleted at c+T; deletion does not undo the effect. An absent record again permits execution. Request handling, record deletion and effect commits have a per-key linearizable order consistent with service time. The suppressing-state check and actual effect are in the same atomic transition: a handler cannot retain an earlier absent observation as authority to execute later. Crashes expose either the entire durable transition or none of it. Service time is monotonic and the retention guarantee survives crashes. These are stipulated implementation properties, stronger than merely having a deduplication table.

reasoning_steps.title: Concrete expiry-induced duplicate after retry issuance stops
reasoning_steps.argument: Take T=10. At time 0 the client durably stores (operation,k,p) and sends request r1. At time 1, r1 commits one effect and D, so C=1; its acknowledgment is lost. At time 2 the client sends same-key retry r2. At time 3 it stops issuing retries, but r2 remains in flight. At time 11, D expires and is deleted. At time 12, r2 reaches its atomic execution transition, finds no D and commits another effect plus a new D, giving C=2. Both commits are atomic, the payload and key never change, and no concurrency or additional crash is needed. The chain is lost acknowledgment → retry already issued → client stops → suppression evidence expires → delayed execution → duplicate effect. This refutes the expiry-only candidate, not the earlier theorem with permanent retention.

reasoning_steps.title: Separate issuance, arrival and effective execution horizons
reasoning_steps.argument: Let S bound final request issuance, A bound final service ingress, and L bound every possible effect-capable atomic execution transition for this operation. An issuance bound S supplies neither A nor L without additional guarantees. Even A alone is insufficient: in the preceding trace, let r2 enter a service queue at time 2.5 but execute at time 12. Then every request has arrived before D expires, yet duplication still occurs. For a concrete sufficient timing construction, suppose all producers cease issuance by S, every transmitted copy arrives or is permanently discarded within Δ, and every arrived request commits its effect-capable transition or becomes irrevocably unable to execute within P of ingress. These bounds must include transport retries, queues, transaction retries, crashes and resumed work. Then A=S+Δ and L=S+Δ+P are valid upper bounds. A client timeout or an unacknowledged cancellation request establishes none of these server-side properties.

reasoning_steps.title: State sufficient contract A: retention dominates execution horizon
reasoning_steps.argument: In addition to the common atomic/stable-key premises, suppose no effect-capable transition for this operation can occur after a finite L. Every first committed effect at c must leave D available through all such later transitions; with deletion allowed at c+T, the strict condition c+T>L suffices. A configuration rule not requiring knowledge of c is: choose a known lower bound b on the first possible effect time and require b+T>L. Since c>=b, this implies c+T>L. For example, b can be the operation's earliest permitted send time, provided no earlier request can exist. Combining this with the previous timing construction gives the conservative rule T>S+Δ+P-b. These are sufficient conditions, not necessary conditions for every possible request schedule.

reasoning_steps.title: Prove contract A, including boundary cases
reasoning_steps.argument: If there is no committed effect, C=0 and safety holds. Otherwise let c be the first effect commit. Suppose a second effect commits at d in the per-key order. The execution-horizon premise gives d<=L, and retention gives L<c+T. The first commit installed D atomically; D cannot be deleted before c+T. Thus D is present at the second transition, which must suppress the effect, a contradiction. Overlapping requests cannot evade this argument because their atomic transitions are ordered and recheck suppressing state. After expiry there is no remaining effect-capable transition by the horizon premise. Crashes preserve the durable record and cannot create a partial commit. Equality needs explicit treatment: if c+T=L and deletion precedes a request at that same timestamp, a duplicate is possible. Strict inequality avoids relying on an unspecified tie order. Concurrent transitions at the same timestamp remain ordered by linearizability.

reasoning_steps.title: State sufficient contract B: retain suppression, expire only the result
reasoning_steps.argument: Alternatively, keep a durable tombstone B(k,p) indefinitely. The first successful execution atomically commits the actual effect, B and the full completion record D. Every effect-capable transition checks B within the same atomic transition: if B exists, it performs no effect; mismatching payloads are rejected. D may expire after T, but B is never removed, forgotten during failover, or bypassed by a worker. After D expires, a matching request may receive an explicit 'already applied; original result unavailable' response rather than a fabricated success receipt. All execution paths, including overlapping or resumed handlers, obey this gate. This branch does not require any bound on request delay.

reasoning_steps.title: Prove contract B by invariant
reasoning_steps.argument: Initially C=0 and B is absent. Induct over the linearized durable transitions. A rejected or suppressed request changes neither C nor B. A first successful request with B absent atomically changes (C,B) from (0,absent) to (1,present). No request with B present can increment C. Expiring D leaves B unchanged, and crashes preserve the durable state or leave an interrupted transaction uncommitted. Hence every finite execution prefix satisfies C∈{0,1} and B is present exactly when C=1. Arbitrarily late requests therefore cannot create a second effect. Installing B only after the effect would reopen the effect-before-record crash window; allowing any gap between deleting D and installing B would likewise invalidate this proof. Atomic installation at the original effect commit avoids both gaps.

reasoning_steps.title: Distinguish safe cessation, cancellation and verified completion
reasoning_steps.argument: Stopping retry issuance constrains future client sends, not requests already transmitted, queued or executing. To assert that no effect can occur after a cancellation acknowledgment, the service needs an additional contract: cancellation must fence every execution path at its atomic effect transition, and any already-committed effect must be reported rather than treated as cancelled. Merely stopping an agent or restoring a checkpoint does not provide that contract. Both proved branches establish only at-most-once safety. They permit C=0 forever, and neither guarantees truthful client completion by a deadline. In contract B, loss of D can remove result retrievability without removing duplicate suppression. Regenerating a key to recover a missing result remains unsafe. Consequently duplicate rate, omission rate, result availability and post-stop effects must be separate evaluation outcomes.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify the next falsification test and its limits
reasoning_steps.argument: When execution becomes available, prioritize a deterministic expiry-boundary test: reproduce the time-1/time-12 commits with T=10, then move the delayed request before, exactly at and after time 11. Test both network delay and pre-expiry ingress followed by queue delay. Compare expiry-only, horizon-covered retention and durable-tombstone implementations under the same schedules. Add overlapping requests, crashes at first commit and D expiry, and failover with tombstone persistence. Independently count external effects and log issuance, ingress, atomic transition, expiry, cancellation acknowledgment and result availability. A second effect under a claimed sufficient contract falsifies implementation compliance or a timing premise; no observed duplicates in a finite test would not prove the general theorem or establish deployment rates. The analytical trace predicts a discriminator but is not an executed result.

reasoning_steps.title: Define finite retention, execution and concurrency
reasoning_steps.argument: One initially unperformed logical operation has a fixed payload p and a durably assigned key k. Every execution path for it uses k; keys are not reused. C counts all actual irreversible effects for the operation. A successful first execution at service time c atomically increments C and creates completion record D(k,p). Under the expiry-only implementation, D suppresses effects during [c,c+T), where T>0, and may be deleted at c+T; deletion does not undo the effect. An absent record again permits execution. Request handling, record deletion and effect commits have a per-key linearizable order consistent with service time. The suppressing-state check and actual effect are in the same atomic transition: a handler cannot retain an earlier absent observation as authority to execute later. Crashes expose either the entire durable transition or none of it. Service time is monotonic and the retention guarantee survives crashes. These are stipulated implementation properties, stronger than merely having a deduplication table.

review.rationale: These are explicit premises of the conditional claim. Atomic checking with the actual effect, per-key ordering of deletion, crash durability, and monotonic retention time make the later concurrency and expiry arguments well-defined. They are not evidence that any deployed interface satisfies this model.

reasoning_steps.title: Concrete expiry-induced duplicate after retry issuance stops
reasoning_steps.argument: Take T=10. At time 0 the client durably stores (operation,k,p) and sends request r1. At time 1, r1 commits one effect and D, so C=1; its acknowledgment is lost. At time 2 the client sends same-key retry r2. At time 3 it stops issuing retries, but r2 remains in flight. At time 11, D expires and is deleted. At time 12, r2 reaches its atomic execution transition, finds no D and commits another effect plus a new D, giving C=2. Both commits are atomic, the payload and key never change, and no concurrency or additional crash is needed. The chain is lost acknowledgment → retry already issued → client stops → suppression evidence expires → delayed execution → duplicate effect. This refutes the expiry-only candidate, not the earlier theorem with permanent retention.

reasoning_steps.title: Separate issuance, arrival and effective execution horizons
reasoning_steps.argument: Let S bound final request issuance, A bound final service ingress, and L bound every possible effect-capable atomic execution transition for this operation. An issuance bound S supplies neither A nor L without additional guarantees. Even A alone is insufficient: in the preceding trace, let r2 enter a service queue at time 2.5 but execute at time 12. Then every request has arrived before D expires, yet duplication still occurs. For a concrete sufficient timing construction, suppose all producers cease issuance by S, every transmitted copy arrives or is permanently discarded within Δ, and every arrived request commits its effect-capable transition or becomes irrevocably unable to execute within P of ingress. These bounds must include transport retries, queues, transaction retries, crashes and resumed work. Then A=S+Δ and L=S+Δ+P are valid upper bounds. A client timeout or an unacknowledged cancellation request establishes none of these server-side properties.

review.rationale: A request admitted at 2.5 can remain queued until 12, so an ingress bound does not bound execution. Under the stronger universal transport and processing bounds, issuance by S implies ingress or permanent discard by S+Δ and execution or irreversible disabling by S+Δ+P. Including every producer, retry, and resumed handler is essential and is explicitly required.

reasoning_steps.title: State sufficient contract A: retention dominates execution horizon
reasoning_steps.argument: In addition to the common atomic/stable-key premises, suppose no effect-capable transition for this operation can occur after a finite L. Every first committed effect at c must leave D available through all such later transitions; with deletion allowed at c+T, the strict condition c+T>L suffices. A configuration rule not requiring knowledge of c is: choose a known lower bound b on the first possible effect time and require b+T>L. Since c>=b, this implies c+T>L. For example, b can be the operation's earliest permitted send time, provided no earlier request can exist. Combining this with the previous timing construction gives the conservative rule T>S+Δ+P-b. These are sufficient conditions, not necessary conditions for every possible request schedule.

review.rationale: This is a sufficient-contract premise, not an established timing property. Given c>=b, b+T>L entails c+T>L. Substituting L=S+Δ+P yields the stated conservative rule. The claim is explicitly conditional on these listed premises.

reasoning_steps.title: Prove contract A, including boundary cases
reasoning_steps.argument: If there is no committed effect, C=0 and safety holds. Otherwise let c be the first effect commit. Suppose a second effect commits at d in the per-key order. The execution-horizon premise gives d<=L, and retention gives L<c+T. The first commit installed D atomically; D cannot be deleted before c+T. Thus D is present at the second transition, which must suppress the effect, a contradiction. Overlapping requests cannot evade this argument because their atomic transitions are ordered and recheck suppressing state. After expiry there is no remaining effect-capable transition by the horizon premise. Crashes preserve the durable record and cannot create a partial commit. Equality needs explicit treatment: if c+T=L and deletion precedes a request at that same timestamp, a duplicate is possible. Strict inequality avoids relying on an unspecified tie order. Concurrent transitions at the same timestamp remain ordered by linearizability.

review.rationale: Any second effect would have an ordered transition at d<=L<c+T, while the first suppressing record is still available. The mandatory atomic check therefore forbids it. Same-timestamp transitions remain ordered, and the equality example correctly identifies a possible deletion-before-execution race when strict inequality is dropped.

reasoning_steps.title: State sufficient contract B: retain suppression, expire only the result
reasoning_steps.argument: Alternatively, keep a durable tombstone B(k,p) indefinitely. The first successful execution atomically commits the actual effect, B and the full completion record D. Every effect-capable transition checks B within the same atomic transition: if B exists, it performs no effect; mismatching payloads are rejected. D may expire after T, but B is never removed, forgotten during failover, or bypassed by a worker. After D expires, a matching request may receive an explicit 'already applied; original result unavailable' response rather than a fabricated success receipt. All execution paths, including overlapping or resumed handlers, obey this gate. This branch does not require any bound on request delay.

review.rationale: Permanent tombstone retention, atomic installation with the actual effect, and mandatory checks on every execution path are explicit alternative premises. Expiring only D leaves the suppression gate intact. An explicit result-unavailable response avoids equating duplicate suppression with result recovery.

reasoning_steps.title: Prove contract B by invariant
reasoning_steps.argument: Initially C=0 and B is absent. Induct over the linearized durable transitions. A rejected or suppressed request changes neither C nor B. A first successful request with B absent atomically changes (C,B) from (0,absent) to (1,present). No request with B present can increment C. Expiring D leaves B unchanged, and crashes preserve the durable state or leave an interrupted transaction uncommitted. Hence every finite execution prefix satisfies C∈{0,1} and B is present exactly when C=1. Arbitrarily late requests therefore cannot create a second effect. Installing B only after the effect would reopen the effect-before-record crash window; allowing any gap between deleting D and installing B would likewise invalidate this proof. Atomic installation at the original effect commit avoids both gaps.

review.rationale: Starting from (0,absent), the only incrementing transition atomically reaches (1,present); all later gated transitions preserve it. Record expiry and stipulated crash behavior do not remove B. The invariant therefore holds for every finite prefix, excluding any second effect even with unbounded request delay.

reasoning_steps.title: Distinguish safe cessation, cancellation and verified completion
reasoning_steps.argument: Stopping retry issuance constrains future client sends, not requests already transmitted, queued or executing. To assert that no effect can occur after a cancellation acknowledgment, the service needs an additional contract: cancellation must fence every execution path at its atomic effect transition, and any already-committed effect must be reported rather than treated as cancelled. Merely stopping an agent or restoring a checkpoint does not provide that contract. Both proved branches establish only at-most-once safety. They permit C=0 forever, and neither guarantees truthful client completion by a deadline. In contract B, loss of D can remove result retrievability without removing duplicate suppression. Regenerating a key to recover a missing result remains unsafe. Consequently duplicate rate, omission rate, result availability and post-stop effects must be separate evaluation outcomes.

Then every request has arrived before D expires, yet duplication still occurs. For a concrete sufficient timing construction, suppose all producers cease issuance by S, every transmitted copy arrives or is permanently discarded within Δ, and every arrived request commits its effect-capable transition or becomes irrevocably unable to execute within P of ingress. These bounds must include transport retries, queues, transaction retries, crashes and resumed work. Then A=S+Δ and L=S+Δ+P are valid upper bounds. A client timeout or an unacknowledged cancellation request establishes none of these server-side properties.

review.rationale: A request admitted at 2.5 can remain queued until 12, so an ingress bound does not bound execution. Under the stronger universal transport and processing bounds, issuance by S implies ingress or permanent discard by S+Δ and execution or irreversible disabling by S+Δ+P. Including every producer, retry, and resumed handler is essential and is explicitly required.

argument_steps.title: State sufficient contract A: retention dominates execution horizon
argument_steps.argument: In addition to the common atomic/stable-key premises, suppose no effect-capable transition for this operation can occur after a finite L. Every first committed effect at c must leave D available through all such later transitions; with deletion allowed at c+T, the strict condition c+T>L suffices. A configuration rule not requiring knowledge of c is: choose a known lower bound b on the first possible effect time and require b+T>L. Since c>=b, this implies c+T>L. For example, b can be the operation's earliest permitted send time, provided no earlier request can exist. Combining this with the previous timing construction gives the conservative rule T>S+Δ+P-b. These are sufficient conditions, not necessary conditions for every possible request schedule.

review.rationale: This is a sufficient-contract premise, not an established timing property. Given c>=b, b+T>L entails c+T>L. Substituting L=S+Δ+P yields the stated conservative rule. The claim is explicitly conditional on these listed premises.

argument_steps.title: Prove contract A, including boundary cases
argument_steps.argument: If there is no committed effect, C=0 and safety holds. Otherwise let c be the first effect commit. Suppose a second effect commits at d in the per-key order. The execution-horizon premise gives d<=L, and retention gives L<c+T. The first commit installed D atomically; D cannot be deleted before c+T. Thus D is present at the second transition, which must suppress the effect, a contradiction. Overlapping requests cannot evade this argument because their atomic transitions are ordered and recheck suppressing state. After expiry there is no remaining effect-capable transition by the horizon premise. Crashes preserve the durable record and cannot create a partial commit. Equality needs explicit treatment: if c+T=L and deletion precedes a request at that same timestamp, a duplicate is possible. Strict inequality avoids relying on an unspecified tie order. Concurrent transitions at the same timestamp remain ordered by linearizability.

review.rationale: Any second effect would have an ordered transition at d<=L<c+T, while the first suppressing record is still available. The mandatory atomic check therefore forbids it. Same-timestamp transitions remain ordered, and the equality example correctly identifies a possible deletion-before-execution race when strict inequality is dropped.

argument_steps.title: State sufficient contract B: retain suppression, expire only the result
argument_steps.argument: Alternatively, keep a durable tombstone B(k,p) indefinitely. The first successful execution atomically commits the actual effect, B and the full completion record D. Every effect-capable transition checks B within the same atomic transition: if B exists, it performs no effect; mismatching payloads are rejected. D may expire after T, but B is never removed, forgotten during failover, or bypassed by a worker. After D expires, a matching request may receive an explicit 'already applied; original result unavailable' response rather than a fabricated success receipt. All execution paths, including overlapping or resumed handlers, obey this gate. This branch does not require any bound on request delay.

review.rationale: Permanent tombstone retention, atomic installation with the actual effect, and mandatory checks on every execution path are explicit alternative premises. Expiring only D leaves the suppression gate intact. An explicit result-unavailable response avoids equating duplicate suppression with result recovery.

argument_steps.title: Prove contract B by invariant
argument_steps.argument: Initially C=0 and B is absent. Induct over the linearized durable transitions. A rejected or suppressed request changes neither C nor B. A first successful request with B absent atomically changes (C,B) from (0,absent) to (1,present). No request with B present can increment C. Expiring D leaves B unchanged, and crashes preserve the durable state or leave an interrupted transaction uncommitted. Hence every finite execution prefix satisfies C∈{0,1} and B is present exactly when C=1. Arbitrarily late requests therefore cannot create a second effect. Installing B only after the effect would reopen the effect-before-record crash window; allowing any gap between deleting D and installing B would likewise invalidate this proof. Atomic installation at the original effect commit avoids both gaps.

review.rationale: Starting from (0,absent), the only incrementing transition atomically reaches (1,present); all later gated transitions preserve it. Record expiry and stipulated crash behavior do not remove B. The invariant therefore holds for every finite prefix, excluding any second effect even with unbounded request delay.

argument_steps.title: Distinguish safe cessation, cancellation and verified completion
argument_steps.argument: Stopping retry issuance constrains future client sends, not requests already transmitted, queued or executing. To assert that no effect can occur after a cancellation acknowledgment, the service needs an additional contract: cancellation must fence every execution path at its atomic effect transition, and any already-committed effect must be reported rather than treated as cancelled. Merely stopping an agent or restoring a checkpoint does not provide that contract. Both proved branches establish only at-most-once safety. They permit C=0 forever, and neither guarantees truthful client completion by a deadline. In contract B, loss of D can remove result retrievability without removing duplicate suppression. Regenerating a key to recover a missing result remains unsafe. Consequently duplicate rate, omission rate, result availability and post-stop effects must be separate evaluation outcomes.

review.rationale: Neither safety proof forces a first effect or successful response, so omission and incomplete reporting remain possible. Outstanding requests are unaffected by stopping issuance. A cancellation guarantee requires execution fencing beyond the proved contracts; this is correctly identified as an additional requirement, not claimed as proved. Fresh-key recovery also leaves the stated stable-key guarantees.

argument_steps.title: Specify the next falsification test and its limits
argument_steps.argument: When execution becomes available, prioritize a deterministic expiry-boundary test: reproduce the time-1/time-12 commits with T=10, then move the delayed request before, exactly at and after time 11. Test both network delay and pre-expiry ingress followed by queue delay. Compare expiry-only, horizon-covered retention and durable-tombstone implementations under the same schedules. Add overlapping requests, crashes at first commit and D expiry, and failover with tombstone persistence. Independently count external effects and log issuance, ingress, atomic transition, expiry, cancellation acknowledgment and result availability. A second effect under a claimed sufficient contract falsifies implementation compliance or a timing premise; no observed duplicates in a finite test would not prove the general theorem or establish deployment rates. The analytical trace predicts a discriminator but is not an executed result.

review.rationale: The proposed schedules target the demonstrated expiry boundary and the distinction between ingress and execution. Independent effect counts, failover checks, and explicit transition timestamps are appropriate falsifiers. The step correctly treats all tests as unexecuted and finite agreement as insufficient for universal or deployment claims.

reasoning_steps.title: Evidence scope and continuity
reasoning_steps.argument: The supplied bounded extract of 5e47ab12-4c7d-45ae-9b1f-af87a75768d6 specifies A/K with nonexpiring receipts. Its proof relies on never removing the receipt; it does not transfer unchanged to finite retention.
