reasoning_steps.title: Define finite retention and its clock
reasoning_steps.argument: Consider one logical operation, fixed payload x, and one durably preserved key k; C counts all its irreversible external effects. Initially C=0 and no receipt exists. Use one authoritative service clock t, with a consistent ordering of processing and expiration events. It advances through outages, never rolls back across restart, and is coherent across any participating replicas. A first atomic commitment at time c creates the actual durable effect and receipt R[k]=(x, success, c, e), where e=c+T and T>0. The receipt is usable exactly while t<e; at t=e it is expired, even if physical garbage collection is delayed. Replays do not refresh e. Expiration never removes an effect. At a serialized processing transition, the service returns a valid matching receipt without an effect; absent such a receipt, the ordinary finite-retention implementation creates one effect and a new receipt atomically. Payload mismatches against a valid receipt are rejected. There is no other deduplication or repair.

reasoning_steps.title: Define delayed requests and crash recovery
reasoning_steps.argument: A send can be dropped, duplicated, or delayed in transport or service queues. Gateway arrival is not the effect-capable processing time. Any delayed copy may survive a client or service restart. Client recovery restores the same operation key and payload; where used, it also restores the original cutoff and deadline rather than resetting them. Service restart preserves committed effects, unexpired receipts, their original expiration times, and any execution-deadline enforcement. It abandons uncommitted atomic work; durable queues may later redeliver requests. Deduplication checks, execution-eligibility checks, and an effect-producing commit are one serialized transition, with no authorization cached across expiration or deadline passage. Without an additional bound, the last possible processing time of a request is unbounded.

reasoning_steps.title: Construct a stable-key duplication trace
reasoning_steps.argument: Take T=10 clock units. At t=1 the initial request atomically creates one effect and its receipt, so C=1 and e=11. Its acknowledgment is lost, and the client crashes before saving completion. Recovery restores the same (k,x), sends a retry at t=2, and sends nothing after a cutoff S=3. The retry remains queued. A service restart at t=10 preserves the receipt and its original expiry. At t=11 the receipt expires. At t=12 the queued retry is processed: no valid receipt exists, so the ordinary atomic implementation commits another effect and a new receipt, giving C=2. Every send respected S, operation identity remained stable, and each individual effect-plus-receipt commit was atomic. The missing protection is against processing after the original receipt expires.

reasoning_steps.title: State and prove the expiry-coverage safety condition
reasoning_steps.argument: A sufficient condition is: after the first commitment at c, every later attempt either processes while its original receipt remains valid, or is forbidden from creating an effect. To prove safety, suppose a first duplicate occurs at p. If p<c+T, the original receipt is still valid and the atomic replay rule forbids an effect, a contradiction. If p>=c+T, the additional condition forbids an effect, also a contradiction. Crashes expose neither split durable states nor a bypass of the checks. Thus every finite execution prefix has C<=1, and an infinite execution cannot have a violation without a finite first violation. The old equivalence 'receipt present iff C=1' must be dropped: after expiry C=1 with no valid receipt is allowed. The replacement invariant is C<=1 together with the requirement that an expired, previously committed operation cannot again be effect-eligible. This requirement must be enforced by a concrete contract, not inferred from the client's uncertainty.

reasoning_steps.title: Sufficient contract A: bound the last possible processing
reasoning_steps.argument: Let a be a known service-clock lower bound on any first commitment, established before sending. Suppose all original requests, retries, and automatically redelivered copies are sent by service-clock time S. Further require that each copy either is permanently discarded or has its final effect-capable processing transition no later than its send time plus Δ. This bound includes transport, queues, outages, restart, and processing stalls—not just network arrival. Then L=S+Δ bounds the last possible effect-capable processing time. Require L<a+T, with strict inequality because processing at expiry is unsafe in the ordinary service. Since a first commitment satisfies c>=a, L<a+T<=c+T; every later possible execution therefore occurs before receipt expiry and is deduplicated. This proves at-most-once safety under the stated processing bound. If a client's cutoff clock has a known upper conversion error ε, replace S by S_client+ε. Without a finite Δ or an equivalent discard rule, a send cutoff does not bound L, and the preceding duplication trace applies. A restarted client that resets S also violates this contract.

reasoning_steps.title: Sufficient contract B: service-enforced rejection without a delay bound
reasoning_steps.argument: Before the first send, bind k and x to an authoritative, immutable validity interval [a,D), with 0<D-a<=T. The service can validate that binding even after deleting the receipt. No recovery or credential reissue may extend D or substitute a fresh key for this logical operation. At the atomic processing transition, a valid receipt may be returned without an effect; otherwise a new effect is permitted only if a<=t<D. At t>=D the service must reject effect creation, including requests admitted or queued before D. Restart and replica failover must preserve this rule. Any first commitment has c>=a, hence its expiry e=c+T>=a+T>=D. A supposed duplicate at p<D encounters the valid original receipt because p<D<=e; at p>=D it is rejected by the execution gate. Therefore C<=1 without any delivery-delay bound. The equality D=a+T is safe because the gate rejects at D, whereas the ordinary service would allow a new effect at receipt expiry. This is a sufficient contract, not a claim that deadline tokens are the only solution; durable tombstones or other fencing protocols require their own analysis.

reasoning_steps.title: Explain completion, reporting, and safe stopping
reasoning_steps.argument: Neither sufficient contract guarantees completion. Under contract B, if every request is lost or reaches effect-capable processing only at t>=D, C remains zero even if delivery is eventually reliable. Completion requires a successful eligible commitment before D; truthful reporting additionally requires receipt delivery or another authoritative observation. If a committed receipt expires before acknowledgment, an 'expired/unknown' response must not be interpreted as proof of either failure or success. A client that stops sending has not canceled already queued requests. Under contract B, only passage of the enforced service deadline establishes that such requests cannot create later effects; before D they may still commit. Retrying after D under a new key to improve completion sacrifices this proof. Longer windows can preserve more recovery opportunities but require correspondingly longer retention under this construction; their storage, latency, and cost effects remain unmeasured. Safe escalation is a separate outcome, not verified task success.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify an expiry-boundary discriminator
reasoning_steps.argument: Proposed deterministic test, not executed: use independent cloned fixtures, integer clock ticks, a=c=1, T=10, e=D=11, one initial committed effect, lost acknowledgment, stable-key recovery, and a retry sent at t=2. Process the retry at p=10,11,12 in separate fixtures. Ordinary finite retention predicts final C values 1,2,2, with a cached response only at p=10. The service-deadline contract predicts 1,1,1, with cached success at p=10 and expired/unknown rejection at p=11 and p=12. In matched zero-initial-effect controls, ordinary retention predicts C=1 at each processing time; the deadline contract predicts 1,0,0. These controls distinguish genuine rejection from a test harness that never executes retries. Include gateway admission before D followed by processing after D: an ingress-only deadline check must not count as compliant. Repeat with restart spanning expiry, a deliberately rolled-back clock as a negative control, and multiple queued copies. An independent append-only audit ledger should count actual effects by logical operation identity, not by retry key or receipt existence. Record processing time, gate decision, expiry, effect count, response truthfulness, attempts, and recovery outcome. For contract A, classify any processing after L as a violated premise, not a counterexample to its conditional theorem.

reasoning_steps.title: Assess the architectural contribution
reasoning_steps.argument: The evidence table currently has three analytical entries: ordinary A/K with finite retention admits the constructed duplicate; A/K plus a bounded-processing contract prevents duplication under its strong timing premise; A/K plus a persistent service execution gate prevents duplication under unbounded request delay but can reject an operation that never committed. No entry has an implemented mechanism, measured effect size, audited real-tool contract, or cost estimate. This advances the retention/expiry component of the contract-validation obligation and supplies a discriminating experiment, but does not resolve that empirical obligation, concurrency beyond the serialized model, durable repair, multi-service correctness, or delayed harm. The argument uses standard state-machine safety reasoning; material novelty and empirical generality are not assessed without source access and experiments.

Its proof relies on never removing the receipt; it does not transfer unchanged to finite retention. I retain its local split-write and regenerated-key counterexamples as scope constraints, not refutations of all recovery mechanisms. The earlier 'empty current ledger' wording was incorrect: the ledger is nonempty, and its recorded unresolved statuses are preserved. Original-source inspection remains open; eight findings and forty historical obligations are omitted. The incomplete extract of fdfb1b57-9f8a-451c-b9b4-2cca9cbf618f supplies no expiry evidence, and its withdrawn arbitrary-delivery relaxation is not reused. Peer extract 7d39bad1-603b-43cf-ad04-0d256b837472 likewise assumes records remain available for every possible retry, so it does not settle expiry. Peer f59b1252-c29e-4f4a-a888-f436ab9a93aa concerns frozen-panel auditing, not a service safety contract. Neither peer summary independently verifies this extension.

review.rationale: The supplied cycle-1 argument explicitly requires nonexpiring receipts, so removing that premise requires a new invariant. The peer extracts likewise provide no finite-retention proof. The current ledger is nonempty, and the earlier wording error is explicitly corrected without claiming historical resolution.

reasoning_steps.title: Define finite retention and its clock
reasoning_steps.argument: Consider one logical operation, fixed payload x, and one durably preserved key k; C counts all its irreversible external effects. Initially C=0 and no receipt exists. Use one authoritative service clock t, with a consistent ordering of processing and expiration events. It advances through outages, never rolls back across restart, and is coherent across any participating replicas. A first atomic commitment at time c creates the actual durable effect and receipt R[k]=(x, success, c, e), where e=c+T and T>0. The receipt is usable exactly while t<e; at t=e it is expired, even if physical garbage collection is delayed. Replays do not refresh e. Expiration never removes an effect. At a serialized processing transition, the service returns a valid matching receipt without an effect; absent such a receipt, the ordinary finite-retention implementation creates one effect and a new receipt atomically. Payload mismatches against a valid receipt are rejected. There is no other deduplication or repair.

review.rationale: These are explicit premises of the conditional claim. Logical expiration at t=c+T, no replay refresh, and atomic actual-effect/receipt commitment specify the boundary behavior needed for the trace and proofs; none is presented as a demonstrated service property.

reasoning_steps.title: Define delayed requests and crash recovery
reasoning_steps.argument: A send can be dropped, duplicated, or delayed in transport or service queues. Gateway arrival is not the effect-capable processing time. Any delayed copy may survive a client or service restart. Client recovery restores the same operation key and payload; where used, it also restores the original cutoff and deadline rather than resetting them. Service restart preserves committed effects, unexpired receipts, their original expiration times, and any execution-deadline enforcement. It abandons uncommitted atomic work; durable queues may later redeliver requests. Deduplication checks, execution-eligibility checks, and an effect-producing commit are one serialized transition, with no authorization cached across expiration or deadline passage. Without an additional bound, the last possible processing time of a request is unbounded.

review.rationale: The delayed-copy and restart premises explicitly permit processing long after sending while preserving committed state. Requiring eligibility and deduplication checks at the effect-producing transition excludes stale authorization from the conditional model.

reasoning_steps.title: Construct a stable-key duplication trace
reasoning_steps.argument: Take T=10 clock units. At t=1 the initial request atomically creates one effect and its receipt, so C=1 and e=11. Its acknowledgment is lost, and the client crashes before saving completion. Recovery restores the same (k,x), sends a retry at t=2, and sends nothing after a cutoff S=3. The retry remains queued. A service restart at t=10 preserves the receipt and its original expiry. At t=11 the receipt expires. At t=12 the queued retry is processed: no valid receipt exists, so the ordinary atomic implementation commits another effect and a new receipt, giving C=2. Every send respected S, operation identity remained stable, and each individual effect-plus-receipt commit was atomic. The missing protection is against processing after the original receipt expires.

review.rationale: At t=12 the receipt committed at t=1 is invalid because its expiry is 11. The ordinary service therefore takes its absent-receipt execution branch and increments C from one to two. Stable keys, atomic commits, and the send cutoff all remain satisfied.

reasoning_steps.title: State and prove the expiry-coverage safety condition
reasoning_steps.argument: A sufficient condition is: after the first commitment at c, every later attempt either processes while its original receipt remains valid, or is forbidden from creating an effect. To prove safety, suppose a first duplicate occurs at p. If p<c+T, the original receipt is still valid and the atomic replay rule forbids an effect, a contradiction. If p>=c+T, the additional condition forbids an effect, also a contradiction. Crashes expose neither split durable states nor a bypass of the checks. Thus every finite execution prefix has C<=1, and an infinite execution cannot have a violation without a finite first violation. The old equivalence 'receipt present iff C=1' must be dropped: after expiry C=1 with no valid receipt is allowed. The replacement invariant is C<=1 together with the requirement that an expired, previously committed operation cannot again be effect-eligible. This requirement must be enforced by a concrete contract, not inferred from the client's uncertainty.

review.rationale: A first duplicate before c+T is blocked by the original receipt; one at or after c+T is blocked by the additional eligibility condition. Expiry breaks the old receipt/effect equivalence but not this conditional at-most-once proof. Any infinite-execution violation has a finite first occurrence.

reasoning_steps.title: Sufficient contract A: bound the last possible processing
reasoning_steps.argument: Let a be a known service-clock lower bound on any first commitment, established before sending. Suppose all original requests, retries, and automatically redelivered copies are sent by service-clock time S. Further require that each copy either is permanently discarded or has its final effect-capable processing transition no later than its send time plus Δ. This bound includes transport, queues, outages, restart, and processing stalls—not just network arrival. Then L=S+Δ bounds the last possible effect-capable processing time. Require L<a+T, with strict inequality because processing at expiry is unsafe in the ordinary service. Since a first commitment satisfies c>=a, L<a+T<=c+T; every later possible execution therefore occurs before receipt expiry and is deduplicated. This proves at-most-once safety under the stated processing bound. If a client's cutoff clock has a known upper conversion error ε, replace S by S_client+ε. Without a finite Δ or an equivalent discard rule, a send cutoff does not bound L, and the preceding duplication trace applies. A restarted client that resets S also violates this contract.

review.rationale: Under the stated all-copy processing bound, every possible effect-producing transition is at most S+Δ, which is strictly less than a+T and hence c+T. Thus later attempts encounter the first receipt. The strict inequality is necessary for this ordinary-service construction because expiration occurs at equality.

reasoning_steps.title: Sufficient contract B: service-enforced rejection without a delay bound
reasoning_steps.argument: Before the first send, bind k and x to an authoritative, immutable validity interval [a,D), with 0<D-a<=T. The service can validate that binding even after deleting the receipt. No recovery or credential reissue may extend D or substitute a fresh key for this logical operation. At the atomic processing transition, a valid receipt may be returned without an effect; otherwise a new effect is permitted only if a<=t<D. At t>=D the service must reject effect creation, including requests admitted or queued before D. Restart and replica failover must preserve this rule. Any first commitment has c>=a, hence its expiry e=c+T>=a+T>=D. A supposed duplicate at p<D encounters the valid original receipt because p<D<=e; at p>=D it is rejected by the execution gate. Therefore C<=1 without any delivery-delay bound. The equality D=a+T is safe because the gate rejects at D, whereas the ordinary service would allow a new effect at receipt expiry. This is a sufficient contract, not a claim that deadline tokens are the only solution; durable tombstones or other fencing protocols require their own analysis.

review.rationale: The immutable binding gives c≥a and D≤a+T≤c+T. A supposed duplicate before D therefore encounters a valid receipt; one at or after D fails the execution gate. This handles unbounded request delays and equality at D, conditional on durable, nonrenewable operation binding and atomic enforcement.

reasoning_steps.title: Explain completion, reporting, and safe stopping
reasoning_steps.argument: Neither sufficient contract guarantees completion. Under contract B, if every request is lost or reaches effect-capable processing only at t>=D, C remains zero even if delivery is eventually reliable. Completion requires a successful eligible commitment before D; truthful reporting additionally requires receipt delivery or another authoritative observation. If a committed receipt expires before acknowledgment, an 'expired/unknown' response must not be interpreted as proof of either failure or success. A client that stops sending has not canceled already queued requests. Under contract B, only passage of the enforced service deadline establishes that such requests cannot create later effects; before D they may still commit. Retrying after D under a new key to improve completion sacrifices this proof. Longer windows can preserve more recovery opportunities but require correspondingly longer retention under this construction; their storage, latency, and cost effects remain unmeasured. Safe escalation is a separate outcome, not verified task success.

review.rationale: Rejecting all late executions can leave C=0 despite eventual delivery. Conversely, an expired receipt cannot distinguish omission from an earlier unacknowledged commitment. Stopping sends does not cancel queued copies, and changing keys abandons the proved identity condition. No quantitative tradeoff is inferred.

reasoning_steps.title: Specify an expiry-boundary discriminator
reasoning_steps.argument: Proposed deterministic test, not executed: use independent cloned fixtures, integer clock ticks, a=c=1, T=10, e=D=11, one initial committed effect, lost acknowledgment, stable-key recovery, and a retry sent at t=2. Process the retry at p=10,11,12 in separate fixtures. Ordinary finite retention predicts final C values 1,2,2, with a cached response only at p=10. The service-deadline contract predicts 1,1,1, with cached success at p=10 and expired/unknown rejection at p=11 and p=12. In matched zero-initial-effect controls, ordinary retention predicts C=1 at each processing time; the deadline contract predicts 1,0,0. These controls distinguish genuine rejection from a test harness that never executes retries. Include gateway admission before D followed by processing after D: an ingress-only deadline check must not count as compliant. Repeat with restart spanning expiry, a deliberately rolled-back clock as a negative control, and multiple queued copies. An independent append-only audit ledger should count actual effects by logical operation identity, not by retry key or receipt existence. Record processing time, gate decision, expiry, effect count, response truthfulness, attempts, and recovery outcome. For contract A, classify any processing after L as a violated premise, not a counterexample to its conditional theorem.

review.rationale: Applying the specified transitions yields ordinary-service counts 1,2,2 and deadline-service counts 1,1,1 in committed fixtures, and 1,1,1 versus 1,0,0 in zero-effect controls. Separate fixtures avoid cross-boundary contamination. These are analytical predictions, not computational or empirical observations.

reasoning_steps.title: Assess the architectural contribution
reasoning_steps.argument: The evidence table currently has three analytical entries: ordinary A/K with finite retention admits the constructed duplicate; A/K plus a bounded-processing contract prevents duplication under its strong timing premise; A/K plus a persistent service execution gate prevents duplication under unbounded request delay but can reject an operation that never committed. No entry has an implemented mechanism, measured effect size, audited real-tool contract, or cost estimate. This advances the retention/expiry component of the contract-validation obligation and supplies a discriminating experiment, but does not resolve that empirical obligation, concurrency beyond the serialized model, durable repair, multi-service correctness, or delayed harm. The argument uses standard state-machine safety reasoning; material novelty and empirical generality are not assessed without source access and experiments.

review.rationale: The three entries accurately separate a constructed failure from two conditional safeguards. The supplied evidence contains no implementation or measurements, and the stated remaining limits match the argument's single-operation serialized scope. Novelty and empirical generality are appropriately left unassessed.

objective_review.claim: Conditional on: One logical operation has a fixed payload and a durable stable key; keys and validity metadata are not replaced during recovery, and C counts all irreversible effects for the operation; The actual external effect and its receipt commit atomically under serialized processing; receipt replay, expiration, eligibility checking, and commitment have the transition semantics specified in the argument; The authoritative service clock is coherent and nondecreasing across restarts, advances through outages, and defines receipt validity as t<c+T with no replay refresh; Crashes preserve committed effects, receipts until their original expiry, and enforcement metadata; delayed requests and copies may survive restarts, but cannot bypass checks at their effect-capable processing transition; For sufficient contract A only: first commitment cannot precede a, every send occurs by S, every copy is discarded or processed by send time plus Δ, and S+Δ<a+T; For sufficient contract B only: immutable operation-bound validity [a,D) satisfies 0<D-a<=T, remains verifiable after receipt deletion, cannot be renewed for the same operation, and the service forbids effect creation at processing times t>=D; The duplication trace uses the ordinary finite-retention service without either additional sufficient contract. Completion conclusions require successful eligible commitment and, for truthful reporting, authoritative outcome delivery. Conditional on the Investigator's listed stable-identity, atomicity, clock, restart, and contract-specific timing or validity assumptions, finite receipt retention admits stable-key duplication in the ordinary service. At-most-once safety is restored either by bounding every possible effect-capable processing time strictly before the earliest possible receipt expiry, or by enforcing the specified immutable service-side execution deadline. A client send cutoff alone is insufficient. These results establish neither completion nor measured architectural benefit.
objective_review.argument_summary: Cycle 2, steps 2–3 define expiration and delayed-request semantics. Step 4 commits at t=1, expires the receipt at t=11, and processes a same-key queued retry at t=12, producing a second effect despite a send cutoff. Step 5 proves safety by excluding a first duplicate both before and after expiry. Step 6 supplies that exclusion through S+Δ<a+T≤c+T. Step 7 instead uses D≤a+T≤c+T: a retry before D encounters the receipt, while one at or after D cannot create an effect. Step 8 separates this safety guarantee from eligible commitment and authoritative reporting. Step 9 specifies distinguishing tests without claiming execution.

argument_steps.title: Evidence scope and continuity
argument_steps.argument: The supplied bounded extract of 5e47ab12-4c7d-45ae-9b1f-af87a75768d6 specifies A/K with nonexpiring receipts. Its proof relies on never removing the receipt; it does not transfer unchanged to finite retention. I retain its local split-write and regenerated-key counterexamples as scope constraints, not refutations of all recovery mechanisms. The earlier 'empty current ledger' wording was incorrect: the ledger is nonempty, and its recorded unresolved statuses are preserved. Original-source inspection remains open; eight findings and forty historical obligations are omitted. The incomplete extract of fdfb1b57-9f8a-451c-b9b4-2cca9cbf618f supplies no expiry evidence, and its withdrawn arbitrary-delivery relaxation is not reused. Peer extract 7d39bad1-603b-43cf-ad04-0d256b837472 likewise assumes records remain available for every possible retry, so it does not settle expiry. Peer f59b1252-c29e-4f4a-a888-f436ab9a93aa concerns frozen-panel auditing, not a service safety contract. Neither peer summary independently verifies this extension.

review.rationale: The supplied cycle-1 argument explicitly requires nonexpiring receipts, so removing that premise requires a new invariant. The peer extracts likewise provide no finite-retention proof. The current ledger is nonempty, and the earlier wording error is explicitly corrected without claiming historical resolution.

argument_steps.title: Define finite retention and its clock
argument_steps.argument: Consider one logical operation, fixed payload x, and one durably preserved key k; C counts all its irreversible external effects. Initially C=0 and no receipt exists. Use one authoritative service clock t, with a consistent ordering of processing and expiration events. It advances through outages, never rolls back across restart, and is coherent across any participating replicas. A first atomic commitment at time c creates the actual durable effect and receipt R[k]=(x, success, c, e), where e=c+T and T>0. The receipt is usable exactly while t<e; at t=e it is expired, even if physical garbage collection is delayed. Replays do not refresh e. Expiration never removes an effect. At a serialized processing transition, the service returns a valid matching receipt without an effect; absent such a receipt, the ordinary finite-retention implementation creates one effect and a new receipt atomically. Payload mismatches against a valid receipt are rejected. There is no other deduplication or repair.

review.rationale: These are explicit premises of the conditional claim. Logical expiration at t=c+T, no replay refresh, and atomic actual-effect/receipt commitment specify the boundary behavior needed for the trace and proofs; none is presented as a demonstrated service property.

argument_steps.title: Define delayed requests and crash recovery
argument_steps.argument: A send can be dropped, duplicated, or delayed in transport or service queues. Gateway arrival is not the effect-capable processing time. Any delayed copy may survive a client or service restart. Client recovery restores the same operation key and payload; where used, it also restores the original cutoff and deadline rather than resetting them. Service restart preserves committed effects, unexpired receipts, their original expiration times, and any execution-deadline enforcement. It abandons uncommitted atomic work; durable queues may later redeliver requests. Deduplication checks, execution-eligibility checks, and an effect-producing commit are one serialized transition, with no authorization cached across expiration or deadline passage. Without an additional bound, the last possible processing time of a request is unbounded.

review.rationale: The delayed-copy and restart premises explicitly permit processing long after sending while preserving committed state. Requiring eligibility and deduplication checks at the effect-producing transition excludes stale authorization from the conditional model.

argument_steps.title: Construct a stable-key duplication trace
argument_steps.argument: Take T=10 clock units. At t=1 the initial request atomically creates one effect and its receipt, so C=1 and e=11. Its acknowledgment is lost, and the client crashes before saving completion. Recovery restores the same (k,x), sends a retry at t=2, and sends nothing after a cutoff S=3. The retry remains queued. A service restart at t=10 preserves the receipt and its original expiry. At t=11 the receipt expires. At t=12 the queued retry is processed: no valid receipt exists, so the ordinary atomic implementation commits another effect and a new receipt, giving C=2. Every send respected S, operation identity remained stable, and each individual effect-plus-receipt commit was atomic. The missing protection is against processing after the original receipt expires.

review.rationale: At t=12 the receipt committed at t=1 is invalid because its expiry is 11. The ordinary service therefore takes its absent-receipt execution branch and increments C from one to two. Stable keys, atomic commits, and the send cutoff all remain satisfied.

argument_steps.title: State and prove the expiry-coverage safety condition
argument_steps.argument: A sufficient condition is: after the first commitment at c, every later attempt either processes while its original receipt remains valid, or is forbidden from creating an effect. To prove safety, suppose a first duplicate occurs at p. If p<c+T, the original receipt is still valid and the atomic replay rule forbids an effect, a contradiction. If p>=c+T, the additional condition forbids an effect, also a contradiction. Crashes expose neither split durable states nor a bypass of the checks. Thus every finite execution prefix has C<=1, and an infinite execution cannot have a violation without a finite first violation. The old equivalence 'receipt present iff C=1' must be dropped: after expiry C=1 with no valid receipt is allowed. The replacement invariant is C<=1 together with the requirement that an expired, previously committed operation cannot again be effect-eligible. This requirement must be enforced by a concrete contract, not inferred from the client's uncertainty.

review.rationale: A first duplicate before c+T is blocked by the original receipt; one at or after c+T is blocked by the additional eligibility condition. Expiry breaks the old receipt/effect equivalence but not this conditional at-most-once proof. Any infinite-execution violation has a finite first occurrence.

argument_steps.title: Sufficient contract A: bound the last possible processing
argument_steps.argument: Let a be a known service-clock lower bound on any first commitment, established before sending. Suppose all original requests, retries, and automatically redelivered copies are sent by service-clock time S. Further require that each copy either is permanently discarded or has its final effect-capable processing transition no later than its send time plus Δ. This bound includes transport, queues, outages, restart, and processing stalls—not just network arrival. Then L=S+Δ bounds the last possible effect-capable processing time. Require L<a+T, with strict inequality because processing at expiry is unsafe in the ordinary service. Since a first commitment satisfies c>=a, L<a+T<=c+T; every later possible execution therefore occurs before receipt expiry and is deduplicated. This proves at-most-once safety under the stated processing bound. If a client's cutoff clock has a known upper conversion error ε, replace S by S_client+ε. Without a finite Δ or an equivalent discard rule, a send cutoff does not bound L, and the preceding duplication trace applies. A restarted client that resets S also violates this contract.

review.rationale: Under the stated all-copy processing bound, every possible effect-producing transition is at most S+Δ, which is strictly less than a+T and hence c+T. Thus later attempts encounter the first receipt. The strict inequality is necessary for this ordinary-service construction because expiration occurs at equality.

argument_steps.title: Sufficient contract B: service-enforced rejection without a delay bound
argument_steps.argument: Before the first send, bind k and x to an authoritative, immutable validity interval [a,D), with 0<D-a<=T. The service can validate that binding even after deleting the receipt. No recovery or credential reissue may extend D or substitute a fresh key for this logical operation. At the atomic processing transition, a valid receipt may be returned without an effect; otherwise a new effect is permitted only if a<=t<D. At t>=D the service must reject effect creation, including requests admitted or queued before D. Restart and replica failover must preserve this rule. Any first commitment has c>=a, hence its expiry e=c+T>=a+T>=D. A supposed duplicate at p<D encounters the valid original receipt because p<D<=e; at p>=D it is rejected by the execution gate. Therefore C<=1 without any delivery-delay bound. The equality D=a+T is safe because the gate rejects at D, whereas the ordinary service would allow a new effect at receipt expiry. This is a sufficient contract, not a claim that deadline tokens are the only solution; durable tombstones or other fencing protocols require their own analysis.

review.rationale: The immutable binding gives c≥a and D≤a+T≤c+T. A supposed duplicate before D therefore encounters a valid receipt; one at or after D fails the execution gate. This handles unbounded request delays and equality at D, conditional on durable, nonrenewable operation binding and atomic enforcement.

argument_steps.title: Explain completion, reporting, and safe stopping
argument_steps.argument: Neither sufficient contract guarantees completion. Under contract B, if every request is lost or reaches effect-capable processing only at t>=D, C remains zero even if delivery is eventually reliable. Completion requires a successful eligible commitment before D; truthful reporting additionally requires receipt delivery or another authoritative observation. If a committed receipt expires before acknowledgment, an 'expired/unknown' response must not be interpreted as proof of either failure or success. A client that stops sending has not canceled already queued requests. Under contract B, only passage of the enforced service deadline establishes that such requests cannot create later effects; before D they may still commit. Retrying after D under a new key to improve completion sacrifices this proof. Longer windows can preserve more recovery opportunities but require correspondingly longer retention under this construction; their storage, latency, and cost effects remain unmeasured. Safe escalation is a separate outcome, not verified task success.

review.rationale: Rejecting all late executions can leave C=0 despite eventual delivery. Conversely, an expired receipt cannot distinguish omission from an earlier unacknowledged commitment. Stopping sends does not cancel queued copies, and changing keys abandons the proved identity condition. No quantitative tradeoff is inferred.

argument_steps.title: Specify an expiry-boundary discriminator
argument_steps.argument: Proposed deterministic test, not executed: use independent cloned fixtures, integer clock ticks, a=c=1, T=10, e=D=11, one initial committed effect, lost acknowledgment, stable-key recovery, and a retry sent at t=2. Process the retry at p=10,11,12 in separate fixtures. Ordinary finite retention predicts final C values 1,2,2, with a cached response only at p=10. The service-deadline contract predicts 1,1,1, with cached success at p=10 and expired/unknown rejection at p=11 and p=12. In matched zero-initial-effect controls, ordinary retention predicts C=1 at each processing time; the deadline contract predicts 1,0,0. These controls distinguish genuine rejection from a test harness that never executes retries. Include gateway admission before D followed by processing after D: an ingress-only deadline check must not count as compliant. Repeat with restart spanning expiry, a deliberately rolled-back clock as a negative control, and multiple queued copies. An independent append-only audit ledger should count actual effects by logical operation identity, not by retry key or receipt existence. Record processing time, gate decision, expiry, effect count, response truthfulness, attempts, and recovery outcome. For contract A, classify any processing after L as a violated premise, not a counterexample to its conditional theorem.

review.rationale: Applying the specified transitions yields ordinary-service counts 1,2,2 and deadline-service counts 1,1,1 in committed fixtures, and 1,1,1 versus 1,0,0 in zero-effect controls. Separate fixtures avoid cross-boundary contamination. These are analytical predictions, not computational or empirical observations.

argument_steps.title: Assess the architectural contribution
argument_steps.argument: The evidence table currently has three analytical entries: ordinary A/K with finite retention admits the constructed duplicate; A/K plus a bounded-processing contract prevents duplication under its strong timing premise; A/K plus a persistent service execution gate prevents duplication under unbounded request delay but can reject an operation that never committed. No entry has an implemented mechanism, measured effect size, audited real-tool contract, or cost estimate. This advances the retention/expiry component of the contract-validation obligation and supplies a discriminating experiment, but does not resolve that empirical obligation, concurrency beyond the serialized model, durable repair, multi-service correctness, or delayed harm. The argument uses standard state-machine safety reasoning; material novelty and empirical generality are not assessed without source access and experiments.

review.rationale: The three entries accurately separate a constructed failure from two conditional safeguards. The supplied evidence contains no implementation or measurements, and the stated remaining limits match the argument's single-operation serialized scope. Novelty and empirical generality are appropriately left unassessed.

The cycle-3 cancellation theorem is convincing under its explicit premises. The key invariant is PENDING or CANCELLED implies N=0, while APPLIED implies N=1. Discriminating analytical outcomes are an invariant for the stipulated contract and explicit violating traces when its gating, acknowledgment, or retention premises are removed. reasoning_steps.title: 1. Define the operation and the safety boundary
reasoning_steps.argument: Fix one logical operation o with immutable payload p and stable key k, initially unperformed. All retries, restored agents, queues, and repair workers preserve this identity. Let N count its actual irreversible effects, across all execution paths. Its durable service state S is PENDING, APPLIED, or CANCELLED. PENDING means no effect has committed, not merely that a client lacks an acknowledgment. The modeled effect is the actual durable outcome, not an outbox insertion or dispatch intention. Actions outside this boundary and downstream delayed harms are not covered.

reasoning_steps.title: 2. State the crash and concurrency contract
reasoning_steps.argument: For k, state tests, terminal decisions, and the actual effect have a linearizable order consistent with completed calls. The effect and APPLIED record commit indivisibly and durably. Cancellation commits CANCELLED durably before its success response is sent. Crashes and failover preserve committed terminal states; an interrupted transition has either no durable outcome or its complete durable outcome. Every effect-capable path must use this same gate at commitment: an earlier read of PENDING is never a transferable execution authorization. Terminal states are not reset or deleted in the baseline contract.

reasoning_steps.title: 3. Specify the complete transition and response table
reasoning_steps.argument: For a matching key and payload: from PENDING, Execute atomically performs one effect and sets APPLIED, returning APPLIED only after durable commitment; Cancel atomically sets CANCELLED without an effect, returning CANCELLED only after durable commitment. From APPLIED, Execute replays APPLIED without another effect, and Cancel returns ALREADY_APPLIED without changing state. From CANCELLED, both Execute and Cancel return CANCELLED without an effect. Status returns the authoritative state but does not turn PENDING into a cancellation decision. Payload conflicts and invalid authorization return errors without effects. A timeout or disconnected call has outcome UNKNOWN to the caller, not CANCELLED.

reasoning_steps.title: 4. Handle cancellation before execution registration
reasoning_steps.argument: The main theorem starts with a durable PENDING record and a client mapping to k established before any send. To support reordered cancellation arriving before registration, initialization must also be atomic: an authorized Cancel on an absent k installs a bound CANCELLED tombstone; registration and execution must never overwrite it. Equivalently, absent-key cancellation may return UNKNOWN or NOT_REGISTERED without the strong guarantee. Returning CANCELLED for an absent key without installing suppression is unsafe: the delayed original registration can subsequently create PENDING and execute. Keys cannot be reused, and the operation binding must be checked.

reasoning_steps.title: 5. Prove the invariant
reasoning_steps.argument: The invariant is (S=PENDING implies N=0), (S=CANCELLED implies N=0), and (S=APPLIED implies N=1). Initially S=PENDING and N=0. The only effect-producing transition changes (PENDING,0) to (APPLIED,1) atomically. Cancellation changes (PENDING,0) to (CANCELLED,0). All terminal-state calls, status observations, errors, and queue operations leave S and N unchanged. A crash preserves the preceding committed state or the full next state, so it also preserves the invariant. These cases exhaust the stipulated transitions; induction proves the invariant for every finite history prefix, with any number of workers or crashes. Atomic absent-key cancellation, if supported, initializes (CANCELLED,0) and preserves the same argument.

reasoning_steps.title: 6. Enumerate effect–cancellation races
reasoning_steps.argument: Starting in PENDING, exactly three classes of committed outcome exist. Cancel wins first: S=CANCELLED, N=0; every subsequent Execute is suppressed. Execute wins first: S=APPLIED, N=1; cancellation returns ALREADY_APPLIED. Neither commits: S=PENDING, N=0; neither outcome has been established and a later transition may win. Concurrent calls reduce to these classes by linearizability. A cancellation request sent earlier can lose if its transition commits later; request time, queue order, and a worker's earlier PENDING read do not determine the winner. Multiple cancellations replay CANCELLED; multiple executions cannot add effects after the first APPLIED commit.

reasoning_steps.title: 7. Enumerate crash and acknowledgment boundaries
reasoning_steps.argument: Crash before a terminal commit: the durable state remains PENDING, unless the competing call commits; retry or lookup must discover the eventual winner. Crash during either atomic transition: recovery exposes only its precommit or complete postcommit state, never an effect with PENDING or CANCELLED. Cancel commits, then crash or response loss: CANCELLED persists, N=0, and retry returns CANCELLED. Execute commits, then crash or response loss: APPLIED persists, N=1, Execute replays APPLIED and Cancel returns ALREADY_APPLIED. Response received, then client crashes before checkpointing it: the service terminal state still persists; restored clients reuse k and recover the same classification. Lost responses create uncertainty, not permission to report cancellation. These cases cover each transition's before, during, after-commit/before-response, and after-response/client-persistence boundaries; further crashes repeat the same cases.

reasoning_steps.title: 8. Prove what a CANCELLED acknowledgment establishes
reasoning_steps.argument: A valid CANCELLED response is sent only after committing or authoritatively observing S=CANCELLED. The invariant then gives N=0. CANCELLED is absorbing, and the only effect transition requires PENDING, so no later transition can increase N. Every finite later prefix therefore still has N=0, excluding an effect at any later event, including execution by a queued, overlapping, resumed, or repair worker that obeys the gate. By contrast, ALREADY_APPLIED implies S=APPLIED and N=1: cancellation lost and cannot undo the irreversible effect. The contract guarantees no additional execution in that state, but does not certify that the existing effect was desired or harmless.

reasoning_steps.title: 9. Exhibit failures of stopping and unfenced acknowledgments
reasoning_steps.argument: Client-stop trace: a request is queued while S=PENDING; the client stops; the service later commits Execute, giving N=1. Thus stopping alone excludes no later effect. Unfenced-check trace: worker W reads PENDING and pauses; Cancel writes CANCELLED and acknowledges; W resumes and performs an effect without an atomic current-state test. This produces N=1 after the acknowledgment. Premature-response trace: Cancel acknowledges before durable commitment, crashes and loses its cancellation write; a surviving request executes. A transaction covering only cancellation metadata and an outbox does not eliminate either problem if the downstream actual effect remains independently executable. These are constructed counterexamples to weakened contracts, not observed failure rates.

reasoning_steps.title: 10. Derive cancellation-tombstone retention requirements
reasoning_steps.argument: Suppose cancellation commits at x, its tombstone is deleted at d, and absence again permits registration or execution. A request held until after d can then recreate PENDING and execute. Hence no fixed finite TTL alone establishes perpetual exclusion when executable requests may survive arbitrarily long. Sufficient alternatives are: retain the bound CANCELLED suppression indefinitely; replace it atomically with equally durable rejection metadata checked by every effect path; or prove that no path can execute after a finite horizon L and retain suppression through every possible execution time. If execution is possible at L and availability is [x,d), d>L is a sufficient boundary rule. Another sufficient rule is an immutable, nonrenewable operation deadline D, enforced at the actual effect transition, with suppression retained until d>=D and execution forbidden for t>=D. The deadline must remain verifiable after deletion and across restart. Client retry cutoffs, average latency, and a timeout do not establish these premises. Removing bulky response data is permissible if the terminal rejection and operation binding remain. Preserving CANCELLED versus ALREADY_APPLIED classification for arbitrarily late queries additionally requires retained outcome evidence or an honest UNKNOWN response after evidence expires.

reasoning_steps.argument: Handoff 90ffb7c5-eeaa-4090-a206-e7ddcc206707 cites peer source db6d3f8e-de46-4162-bbac-d615d3092afa and target 7d39bad1-603b-43cf-ad04-0d256b837472. I inspected the supplied source extract and the target pointer and ledger scope descriptions; the target original is unavailable, so its full proof has not been inspected. The reported target premise keeps completion records available for every retry. The source explicitly removes that protection and allows execution after expiry unless bounded processing or an execution deadline intervenes. The shared one-operation, stable-key, actual-effect domain matches, but retention premises differ: effect; receipt expiry; delayed retry; second effect is outside the target premise, not a contradiction. Independently, that trace follows by allowing an absent record to authorize execution after deletion. I adopt the complements interpretation provisionally and reject transferring it as a refutation. It changes the next test by requiring cancellation-tombstone deletion crossed with resumed-worker and deadline enforcement cases. The peer's serialized completion-record argument is not proof of concurrent cancellation; steps 5–10 provide the separate conditional argument here.

reasoning_steps.title: 12. Separate safety, progress, and historical limitations
reasoning_steps.argument: The contract proves a safety statement, not that cancellation wins, a response arrives, or the task completes by a deadline H. Eventual discovery additionally needs service progress, delivery of a retry or lookup, and durable client recording; a bound by H needs explicit timing bounds. The supplied historical extract's delivery-relaxation error is not reused: issuing a retry does not imply it commits, so Pr(success in the already-committed history)<=1-q requires the stated retry-commit premise. Other peer work on frozen-roster auditing supplies no service-compliance evidence; the older architectural extract supplies no cancellation proof. All supplied ledger duties concerning implementation audits, empirical comparisons, ungated repair, compensation, and multi-service composition remain unresolved. This cycle supplies a standalone one-operation cancellation argument only, not verification of amendments to unavailable historical artifacts.

reasoning_steps.title: 1. Define the operation and the safety boundary
reasoning_steps.argument: Fix one logical operation o with immutable payload p and stable key k, initially unperformed. All retries, restored agents, queues, and repair workers preserve this identity. Let N count its actual irreversible effects, across all execution paths. Its durable service state S is PENDING, APPLIED, or CANCELLED. PENDING means no effect has committed, not merely that a client lacks an acknowledgment. The modeled effect is the actual durable outcome, not an outbox insertion or dispatch intention. Actions outside this boundary and downstream delayed harms are not covered.

review.rationale: This is an explicit premise of the conditional claim. Counting actual effects across all paths and fixing one immutable operation prevents key replacement or an outbox-only event from silently changing the safety property.

reasoning_steps.title: 2. State the crash and concurrency contract
reasoning_steps.argument: For k, state tests, terminal decisions, and the actual effect have a linearizable order consistent with completed calls. The effect and APPLIED record commit indivisibly and durably. Cancellation commits CANCELLED durably before its success response is sent. Crashes and failover preserve committed terminal states; an interrupted transition has either no durable outcome or its complete durable outcome. Every effect-capable path must use this same gate at commitment: an earlier read of PENDING is never a transferable execution authorization. Terminal states are not reset or deleted in the baseline contract.

review.rationale: The conditional claim explicitly assumes this contract. Linearizable eligibility testing at actual-effect commitment, crash atomicity, durable decisions, and universal gating eliminate the stale-authorization and partial-commit cases used later.

reasoning_steps.title: 3. Specify the complete transition and response table
reasoning_steps.argument: For a matching key and payload: from PENDING, Execute atomically performs one effect and sets APPLIED, returning APPLIED only after durable commitment; Cancel atomically sets CANCELLED without an effect, returning CANCELLED only after durable commitment. From APPLIED, Execute replays APPLIED without another effect, and Cancel returns ALREADY_APPLIED without changing state. From CANCELLED, both Execute and Cancel return CANCELLED without an effect. Status returns the authoritative state but does not turn PENDING into a cancellation decision. Payload conflicts and invalid authorization return errors without effects. A timeout or disconnected call has outcome UNKNOWN to the caller, not CANCELLED.

review.rationale: The table covers both operations from each of the three states. Only PENDING Execute creates an effect; terminal replays, errors, and observations do not. Its response semantics distinguish successful cancellation, prior application, and caller uncertainty.

reasoning_steps.title: 4. Handle cancellation before execution registration
reasoning_steps.argument: The main theorem starts with a durable PENDING record and a client mapping to k established before any send. To support reordered cancellation arriving before registration, initialization must also be atomic: an authorized Cancel on an absent k installs a bound CANCELLED tombstone; registration and execution must never overwrite it. Equivalently, absent-key cancellation may return UNKNOWN or NOT_REGISTERED without the strong guarantee. Returning CANCELLED for an absent key without installing suppression is unsafe: the delayed original registration can subsequently create PENDING and execute. Keys cannot be reused, and the operation binding must be checked.

review.rationale: An absent-key success without persistent suppression admits the stated delayed-registration trace. Installing a bound tombstone atomically and prohibiting overwrite closes that trace; returning an explicitly non-guaranteeing response is also consistent.

reasoning_steps.title: 5. Prove the invariant
reasoning_steps.argument: The invariant is (S=PENDING implies N=0), (S=CANCELLED implies N=0), and (S=APPLIED implies N=1). Initially S=PENDING and N=0. The only effect-producing transition changes (PENDING,0) to (APPLIED,1) atomically. Cancellation changes (PENDING,0) to (CANCELLED,0). All terminal-state calls, status observations, errors, and queue operations leave S and N unchanged. A crash preserves the preceding committed state or the full next state, so it also preserves the invariant. These cases exhaust the stipulated transitions; induction proves the invariant for every finite history prefix, with any number of workers or crashes. Atomic absent-key cancellation, if supported, initializes (CANCELLED,0) and preserves the same argument.

review.rationale: The base case holds, the sole effect transition maps (PENDING,0) to (APPLIED,1), cancellation maps it to (CANCELLED,0), and all other stipulated actions preserve the pair. Crash atomicity excludes intermediate durable pairs, completing the induction.

reasoning_steps.title: 6. Enumerate effect–cancellation races
reasoning_steps.argument: Starting in PENDING, exactly three classes of committed outcome exist. Cancel wins first: S=CANCELLED, N=0; every subsequent Execute is suppressed. Execute wins first: S=APPLIED, N=1; cancellation returns ALREADY_APPLIED. Neither commits: S=PENDING, N=0; neither outcome has been established and a later transition may win. Concurrent calls reduce to these classes by linearizability. A cancellation request sent earlier can lose if its transition commits later; request time, queue order, and a worker's earlier PENDING read do not determine the winner. Multiple cancellations replay CANCELLED; multiple executions cannot add effects after the first APPLIED commit.

review.rationale: A linearized history has either cancellation first, execution first, or no committed terminal transition. Absorbing terminal states prevent any later competing call from changing that classification or adding another effect.

reasoning_steps.title: 7. Enumerate crash and acknowledgment boundaries
reasoning_steps.argument: Crash before a terminal commit: the durable state remains PENDING, unless the competing call commits; retry or lookup must discover the eventual winner. Crash during either atomic transition: recovery exposes only its precommit or complete postcommit state, never an effect with PENDING or CANCELLED. Cancel commits, then crash or response loss: CANCELLED persists, N=0, and retry returns CANCELLED. Execute commits, then crash or response loss: APPLIED persists, N=1, Execute replays APPLIED and Cancel returns ALREADY_APPLIED. Response received, then client crashes before checkpointing it: the service terminal state still persists; restored clients reuse k and recover the same classification. Lost responses create uncertainty, not permission to report cancellation. These cases cover each transition's before, during, after-commit/before-response, and after-response/client-persistence boundaries; further crashes repeat the same cases.

review.rationale: Before/during commit reduces to prestate or complete poststate; after commit, lost responses and client-checkpoint crashes cannot erase the service decision. Stable-key recovery therefore preserves classification without claiming that a response must eventually arrive.

reasoning_steps.title: 8. Prove what a CANCELLED acknowledgment establishes
reasoning_steps.argument: A valid CANCELLED response is sent only after committing or authoritatively observing S=CANCELLED. The invariant then gives N=0. CANCELLED is absorbing, and the only effect transition requires PENDING, so no later transition can increase N. Every finite later prefix therefore still has N=0, excluding an effect at any later event, including execution by a queued, overlapping, resumed, or repair worker that obeys the gate. By contrast, ALREADY_APPLIED implies S=APPLIED and N=1: cancellation lost and cannot undo the irreversible effect. The contract guarantees no additional execution in that state, but does not certify that the existing effect was desired or harmless.

review.rationale: An authoritative CANCELLED response entails a committed CANCELLED state. The invariant establishes no previous effect, and absorption plus universal current-state gating excludes every later effect event. ALREADY_APPLIED instead entails N=1.

reasoning_steps.title: 9. Exhibit failures of stopping and unfenced acknowledgments
reasoning_steps.argument: Client-stop trace: a request is queued while S=PENDING; the client stops; the service later commits Execute, giving N=1. Thus stopping alone excludes no later effect. Unfenced-check trace: worker W reads PENDING and pauses; Cancel writes CANCELLED and acknowledges; W resumes and performs an effect without an atomic current-state test. This produces N=1 after the acknowledgment. Premature-response trace: Cancel acknowledges before durable commitment, crashes and loses its cancellation write; a surviving request executes. A transaction covering only cancellation metadata and an outbox does not eliminate either problem if the downstream actual effect remains independently executable. These are constructed counterexamples to weakened contracts, not observed failure rates.

review.rationale: Each trace removes a specific necessary protection and then exhibits an executable effect after stopping or acknowledgment. These are valid counterexamples to the weakened guarantees, not counterexamples to the stipulated contract or measurements of prevalence.

reasoning_steps.title: 10. Derive cancellation-tombstone retention requirements
reasoning_steps.argument: Suppose cancellation commits at x, its tombstone is deleted at d, and absence again permits registration or execution. A request held until after d can then recreate PENDING and execute. Hence no fixed finite TTL alone establishes perpetual exclusion when executable requests may survive arbitrarily long. Sufficient alternatives are: retain the bound CANCELLED suppression indefinitely; replace it atomically with equally durable rejection metadata checked by every effect path; or prove that no path can execute after a finite horizon L and retain suppression through every possible execution time. If execution is possible at L and availability is [x,d), d>L is a sufficient boundary rule. Another sufficient rule is an immutable, nonrenewable operation deadline D, enforced at the actual effect transition, with suppression retained until d>=D and execution forbidden for t>=D. The deadline must remain verifiable after deletion and across restart. Client retry cutoffs, average latency, and a timeout do not establish these premises. Removing bulky response data is permissible if the terminal rejection and operation binding remain. Preserving CANCELLED versus ALREADY_APPLIED classification for arbitrarily late queries additionally requires retained outcome evidence or an honest UNKNOWN response after evidence expires.

review.rationale: If deletion restores eligibility while executable requests remain, a delayed request supplies a violating trace. Persistent rejection or a universally enforced nonrenewable cutoff prevents that transition. The strict endpoint rule for [x,d) correctly covers execution allowed at L; late outcome classification requires separate retained evidence.

reasoning_steps.title: 11. Evaluate the evidence-linked peer handoff without transferring incompatible scope
reasoning_steps.argument: Handoff 90ffb7c5-eeaa-4090-a206-e7ddcc206707 cites peer source db6d3f8e-de46-4162-bbac-d615d3092afa and target 7d39bad1-603b-43cf-ad04-0d256b837472. I inspected the supplied source extract and the target pointer and ledger scope descriptions; the target original is unavailable, so its full proof has not been inspected. The reported target premise keeps completion records available for every retry. The source explicitly removes that protection and allows execution after expiry unless bounded processing or an execution deadline intervenes. The shared one-operation, stable-key, actual-effect domain matches, but retention premises differ: effect; receipt expiry; delayed retry; second effect is outside the target premise, not a contradiction. Independently, that trace follows by allowing an absent record to authorize execution after deletion. I adopt the complements interpretation provisionally and reject transferring it as a refutation. It changes the next test by requiring cancellation-tombstone deletion crossed with resumed-worker and deadline enforcement cases. The peer's serialized completion-record argument is not proof of concurrent cancellation; steps 5–10 provide the separate conditional argument here.

review.rationale: The supplied peer assumptions explicitly permit finite receipt expiry and require serialized processing. The target retention premise is available only as a reported ledger scope. The step appropriately treats complementarity as provisional, rejects a contradiction across different retention premises, and does not import a concurrent cancellation proof.

reasoning_steps.title: 12. Separate safety, progress, and historical limitations
reasoning_steps.argument: The contract proves a safety statement, not that cancellation wins, a response arrives, or the task completes by a deadline H. Eventual discovery additionally needs service progress, delivery of a retry or lookup, and durable client recording; a bound by H needs explicit timing bounds. The supplied historical extract's delivery-relaxation error is not reused: issuing a retry does not imply it commits, so Pr(success in the already-committed history)<=1-q requires the stated retry-commit premise. Other peer work on frozen-roster auditing supplies no service-compliance evidence; the older architectural extract supplies no cancellation proof. All supplied ledger duties concerning implementation audits, empirical comparisons, ungated repair, compensation, and multi-service composition remain unresolved. This cycle supplies a standalone one-operation cancellation argument only, not verification of amendments to unavailable historical artifacts.

However, the claimed historical extract inspection and characterizations of older peer work cannot be checked from pointer-only sources.

argument_steps.title: 9. Exhibit failures of stopping and unfenced acknowledgments
argument_steps.argument: Client-stop trace: a request is queued while S=PENDING; the client stops; the service later commits Execute, giving N=1. Thus stopping alone excludes no later effect. Unfenced-check trace: worker W reads PENDING and pauses; Cancel writes CANCELLED and acknowledges; W resumes and performs an effect without an atomic current-state test. This produces N=1 after the acknowledgment. Premature-response trace: Cancel acknowledges before durable commitment, crashes and loses its cancellation write; a surviving request executes. A transaction covering only cancellation metadata and an outbox does not eliminate either problem if the downstream actual effect remains independently executable. These are constructed counterexamples to weakened contracts, not observed failure rates.

argument_steps.title: 10. Derive cancellation-tombstone retention requirements
argument_steps.argument: Suppose cancellation commits at x, its tombstone is deleted at d, and absence again permits registration or execution. A request held until after d can then recreate PENDING and execute. Hence no fixed finite TTL alone establishes perpetual exclusion when executable requests may survive arbitrarily long. Sufficient alternatives are: retain the bound CANCELLED suppression indefinitely; replace it atomically with equally durable rejection metadata checked by every effect path; or prove that no path can execute after a finite horizon L and retain suppression through every possible execution time. If execution is possible at L and availability is [x,d), d>L is a sufficient boundary rule. Another sufficient rule is an immutable, nonrenewable operation deadline D, enforced at the actual effect transition, with suppression retained until d>=D and execution forbidden for t>=D. The deadline must remain verifiable after deletion and across restart. Client retry cutoffs, average latency, and a timeout do not establish these premises. Removing bulky response data is permissible if the terminal rejection and operation binding remain. Preserving CANCELLED versus ALREADY_APPLIED classification for arbitrarily late queries additionally requires retained outcome evidence or an honest UNKNOWN response after evidence expires.

reasoning_steps.title: 1. Define the operation, time boundaries, and outcome dimensions
reasoning_steps.argument: Consider one initially unperformed logical operation with fixed payload p, stable key k, and immutable authorization interval [a,D), where 0<D-a<=T. Every effect-producing path uses this same identity and authorization. Let C count all actual irreversible effects for this operation, including effects under any erroneously substituted key. An effect committed at service time c creates a receipt valid on [c,c+T); replay does not extend expiry. Safety means C<=1 for every execution prefix, including after D and an evaluation deadline H. Effect completion by H means C(H)=1. Verified task completion additionally requires appropriate authoritative evidence and a truthful report by H; payload/task correctness beyond this single effect remains a separate requirement.

reasoning_steps.title: 2. Cached deduplication admits duplication even before expiry
reasoning_steps.argument: Set a=0, D=T=10. At t=1, workers W1 and W2 independently read 'no receipt' and 'eligible', then pause. At t=2, W1 commits an actual effect and its receipt, giving C=1. At t=3, W2 uses its cached absence decision and unconditionally commits another effect plus replacement receipt, giving C=2. Each effect may be atomic with its own receipt write; what is missing is a current-state conditional decision encompassing that effect. A true atomic absent-key conditional commit would reject or replay W2, so this trace refutes the specified cached-absence implementation, not every implementation that performs preliminary reads.

reasoning_steps.title: 3. Cached deadline authorization admits duplication after legitimate GC
reasoning_steps.argument: Again set a=0, D=T=10. At t=1, W2 caches authorization to execute, but stalls before its authoritative receipt lookup. W1 commits at c=2, giving C=1 and receipt expiry 12; its acknowledgment is lost. At t=12, GC legitimately deletes that expired receipt. At t=13, W2 atomically checks the current receipt state, finds it absent, and commits another effect plus receipt using its cached authorization: C=2. Thus even a current absent-receipt conditional commit is insufficient if deadline authorization can survive beyond D. This trace violates execution-time authorization, not the strengthened contract proposed below.

reasoning_steps.title: 4. Specify the sufficient effect-capable transition
reasoning_steps.argument: B_concurrent requires a per-operation linearizable transition shared by all workers and effect-producing paths. At that transition's actual commitment time t: (i) validate the immutable binding of operation, k, p, a, D, and T, rejecting mismatches; (ii) inspect the current authoritative receipt and its original expiry; (iii) if a matching unexpired committed receipt exists, return that result without an effect; (iv) otherwise, if t is outside [a,D), return NOT_ELIGIBLE_OUTCOME_UNKNOWN without an effect; (v) otherwise atomically commit exactly one actual effect and its matching committed receipt with c=t and expiry c+T. Only branch (v) creates effects. Its eligibility test and absent-valid-receipt test are inseparable from the actual effect and receipt commit. Preliminary reads are advisory, never transferable execution permission. A committed receipt may be replayed after D while still valid, because replay creates no effect.

reasoning_steps.title: 5. Cover expiry, GC, crashes, and physical commitment
reasoning_steps.argument: Receipt lookup, effect commitment, and GC have one consistent per-operation order. Logical expiry is determined by current authoritative time, independently of whether physical deletion has occurred. GC may remove only the currently identified receipt version when t>=c+T; it cannot delete an unexpired receipt, erase authorization enforcement, or install reusable permission. Service time is coherent and nondecreasing across workers, restarts, and failover, and advances through outages. Crashes expose either the entire effect-plus-receipt commit or neither; unexpired receipts survive. Authorization remains verifiable after receipt deletion and cannot be renewed for this operation. Critically, t is the actual irreversible effect commitment time, not ingress time, transaction-start time, or an earlier chosen linearization timestamp. Committing a local intent before D and executing an unguarded downstream effect later does not satisfy this contract.

reasoning_steps.title: 6. Establish retention coverage of the entire eligibility interval
reasoning_steps.argument: If a first effect commits at c, branch (v) implies a<=c<D. Its receipt expires at e=c+T. Since c>=a and T>=D-a, e=c+T>=a+T>=D. Therefore, after the first effect and at every later eligible time t<D, t<e: the first receipt is still valid and cannot legitimately be removed by GC. The equality case e=D is safe because eligibility is strictly t<D and receipt validity is strictly t<e. This is a deduction from the contract, not a claim about any deployed retention guarantee.

reasoning_steps.title: 7. Prove at-most-once under overlapping transitions
reasoning_steps.argument: Initially C=0. Replay, rejection, GC, and crashes cannot increment C. Suppose a first effect commits at c and consider any purported next effect-producing transition at t, ordered after it. If t<D, the retention lemma guarantees the first receipt is present and valid, so the transition must replay rather than create an effect. If t>=D, current eligibility forbids creation even if the receipt has expired or been deleted. Times below a also forbid creation. These cases exhaust all times, contradicting a second effect. Concurrent attempts with equal clock values are still ordered by the atomic per-operation transition: the second observes the first receipt. Crashes preserve the relevant committed state by assumption. Hence C<=1 throughout every history satisfying B_concurrent, without delivery, fairness, bounded-delay, or successful-response assumptions.

reasoning_steps.title: 8. Separate safety from completion and truthful reporting
reasoning_steps.argument: Safety permits C=0: all requests can be dropped, stalled until D, or rejected. Eventual delivery alone cannot ensure completion because delivery may occur only after D. A crash-free valid attempt reaching the specified transition before D either finds the existing committed receipt or creates the first effect, yielding C=1; completion by H additionally requires that effect to have committed by H. Truthful completion reporting requires authoritative matching outcome evidence to reach the client and be durably recorded by the reporting deadline. After receipt deletion, an expired rejection does not distinguish 'never committed' from 'committed but receipt expired'; it must not be reported as definite nonexecution or success. A client may retain an earlier authoritative receipt after server GC. Otherwise an unresolved report or escalation can be truthful and safe without constituting successful completion.

reasoning_steps.title: 9. Specify a deterministic two-worker boundary schedule
reasoning_steps.argument: Use resettable state, an exact logical clock, a=0, D=T=10, and barriers rather than sleeps. At clock 0, let both workers perform advisory reads of an absent receipt and eligible authorization. Pause W2. Let W1's actual atomic transition commit at clock 0; verify C=1 and expiry e=10, then drop its acknowledgment. Run separate resets: A, resume W2 at 9: B_concurrent must replay, whereas the unconditional cached-absence variant can produce C=2. B, resume W2 at 10 with GC ordered before W2's transition: B_concurrent must reject creation and leave C=1; the cached-deadline variant with current absent-receipt lookup can produce C=2. C, reverse the order at clock 10: W2 must treat the physically present receipt as expired, reject creation, and leave C=1; subsequent GC changes no effect count. D, perform GC at 10 and resume W2 at 11: creation remains forbidden. Swap worker names and repeat; also run a no-first-commit control, in which arrival at 10 yields C=0, not fabricated completion. These are specified analytical expectations, not execution results.

reasoning_steps.title: 10. State the test oracle and necessary negative controls
reasoning_steps.argument: A future harness should record actual effect events separately from the deduplication table, including operation identity, payload, and commitment time; otherwise overwriting one receipt could hide two effects. It should check C<=1, every new commit's a<=c<D, original receipt expiry without replay refresh, and each returned/reporting status against the effect history. Include mismatched payloads, attempted key/window renewal, crashes immediately before and after the indivisible commit, post-commit response loss, client receipt-to-checkpoint crashes, and restart with a paused worker. Repeat the 9/10/11 boundary schedule under failover and both GC orders. An oracle generated solely from the same receipt logic is not independent. These tests can expose violations but finite agreement cannot establish universal contract compliance.

reasoning_steps.argument: Handoff dd7cee4b-a2f5-4858-8457-f02880182707 links peer source ced69145-e60c-42ed-bd2c-b39b70905a03 to target 5e47ab12-4c7d-45ae-9b1f-af87a75768d6. I examined the supplied source extract and the target's supplied ledger scope, not either original. The target scope assumes serialized attempts and no expiry; the source adds finite retention and linearizable execution gating. Its expiry trace therefore does not contradict the narrower target claim. The source's contract B is an indefinite tombstone construction, whereas this branch's B_concurrent uses immutable time-bounded authorization; the label B must not imply equivalence. I adopt the distinction between stopping sends and disabling all late effect-capable execution. I leave the peer proof and implementation applicability unverified and reject transferring its conclusions to ingress-only checks. The handoff sharpens the next test to resume a stalled worker after GC and to audit the actual downstream gate; it does not disprove this approach. Under the supplied source's own tombstone premise, a surviving tombstone would instead suppress that late worker.

reasoning_steps.title: 12. Bound the contribution and preserve earlier limitations
reasoning_steps.argument: This result supplies an abstract concurrency extension and discriminating tests for the ledger's overlapping-worker limitation; it does not establish a concurrent implementation. The ledger's split-write, regenerated-key, and unprotected finite-retention counterexamples remain negative constraints on those candidates, not objections to the changed B_concurrent scope.
